legacy_profiles.name: --mamba-block-size
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls the block size (in tokens) for Mamba layer KV cache allocation in hybrid Mamba/Attention models. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend aggressively overrides this value to enforce alignment between attention and Mamba page sizes — a hardware requirement for efficient NPU memory management. When `mamba_cache_mode` is "align" and prefix caching is enabled, `mamba_block_size` is forcibly set equal to `block_size` (patch_mamba_config.py:114). When `mamba_cache_mode` is "all", the value is computed as the LCM of the user-specified (or model-default) chunk size and the kernel block alignment size (128 on 310P), then used to derive the attention block size (patch_mamba_config_310.py:69-73). In kv_transfer scenarios without prefix caching, `mamba_block_size` must be a multiple of `block_size` (platform.py:291). The parameter directly affects: "(1) Mamba cache memory footprint — larger blocks reduce the number" of cached states but increase per-block memory; (2) prefix caching granularity — smaller blocks enable finer-grained cache reuse at the cost of more cache entries; (3) causal_conv1d kernel alignment — values not divisible by 8 cause kernel inefficiency or errors. On Ascend, the effective value is almost always determined by the platform patch rather than the user, making this parameter primarily informational for understanding the computed cache layout.

legacy_profiles.name: --mamba-cache-mode
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
Controls the caching strategy for Mamba (state-space model) layers in hybrid attention-Mamba architectures. On Ascend NPU, this parameter has a critical performance impact because it determines:
1. **Block size alignment**: When set to "align", vllm-ascend forces
   `mamba_block_size` to equal `block_size`, ensuring Mamba state pages and
   attention KV pages have identical sizes. This enables efficient hybrid KV
   cache management and is required for KV transfer (disaggregated prefill).
   When set to "all", the block size is computed from the Mamba chunk size
   and kernel alignment constraints, which can result in very large block
   sizes (e.g., 2048 tokens) — meaning prefixes shorter than the block size
   are never cached, reducing prefix caching effectiveness.

2. **KV transfer compatibility**: vllm-ascend's KV transfer (disaggregated
   prefill) only supports "align" mode. If KV transfer is enabled with a
   hybrid model and mamba_cache_mode is "none", it is automatically
   overridden to "align". Any other value raises an assertion error.

3. **AscendStore compatibility**: The AscendStore hybrid linear-attention
   support requires mamba_cache_mode="align" and raises NotImplementedError
   otherwise.

4. **Scheduling constraints**: "align" mode requires block_size <=
   max_num_batched_tokens, chunked MM input enabled, and is incompatible
   with Model Runner V2 (only V1 supported on Ascend).

5. **Memory overhead**: "align" mode may pad Mamba pages to match attention
   page sizes, increasing memory usage by a small percentage (logged as
   "Padding mamba page size by X%").

6. **Prefix caching behavior**: "all" caches Mamba state at every
   i * block_size position; "align" only caches at the last token of each
   scheduler step when the token is at position i * block_size, reducing
   cache write frequency but potentially missing some cache opportunities.

legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the number of Philox PRNG rounds used for stochastic rounding random number generation in Mamba model cache operations. It is only active when --enable-mamba-cache-stochastic-rounding is set. The value is passed to MambaConfig.stochastic_rounding_philox_rounds (default 0, which uses the Triton default). Higher values improve randomness quality at the cost of additional compute per cache access. The performance impact is limited to Mamba-family models (Mamba, Mamba2, Jamba, etc.) and only when stochastic rounding is enabled. On Ascend NPU, Mamba models are supported but the Mamba backend may differ from Triton — vllm-ascend does not override this parameter, so the upstream behavior applies. The compute overhead scales linearly with the number of rounds, affecting both prefill and decode latency for Mamba cache operations.

legacy_profiles.name: --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the data type of the SSM (State Space Model) state cache in Mamba-family models (Mamba1, Mamba2, GatedDeltaNet). It is consumed by `MambaStateDtypeCalculator._mamba_state_dtype()` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/mamba_utils.py:84-90`, which resolves the SSM state dtype separately from the convolution state dtype. When set to "auto", the SSM state dtype falls back to the value of `--mamba-cache-dtype` (which itself defaults to "auto", ultimately resolving to the model's native dtype). Setting a lower-precision dtype (e.g., float16 instead of float32) reduces the memory footprint of the SSM state cache, which can be significant for large-batch or long-sequence Mamba inference. This directly affects GPU/NPU memory usage and can improve throughput by allowing larger batch sizes. On Ascend NPU, float16 operations are natively accelerated by the Da Vinci architecture, making float16 the recommended choice for production deployments. The parameter also interacts with FlashAttention backend block size selection: "when `mamba_ssm_cache_dtype`" or `mamba_cache_dtype` is float32, the FlashAttention backend restricts supported block sizes to [16, 32, 64] instead of the default MultipleOf(16) to avoid NaN propagation issues (see `vllm/v1/attention/backends/flash_attn.py:86-94`). This block size restriction can reduce KV cache efficiency in hybrid Mamba/Attention models. Additionally, stochastic rounding for Mamba cache requires the SSM cache to be float16; setting any other value with stochastic rounding enabled raises a ValueError (see `vllm/config/vllm.py:778-788`).

legacy_profiles.name: --max-cudagraph-capture-size
legacy_profiles.valid_choices: positive integer, or null to auto-compute
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter sets the upper bound on the number of tokens for which CUDA graph (or NPU equivalent) capture is performed. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend overrides the upstream default computation: "instead of `min(max_num_seqs * 2, 512)`, it uses `min(max_num_seqs *" decode_query_len, 512)` where `decode_query_len = 1 + num_speculative_tokens` (see `_get_default_max_cudagraph_capture_size` in vllm_ascend/platform.py:177-211). This value directly controls: 1. The list of batch sizes for which execution graphs are pre-captured (generated as [1,2,4]
   + multiples of 8 up to 256 + multiples of 16 up to this max).
2. The pre-allocation of MoE token dispatch buffers in `token_dispatcher.py:131` — the
   `max_num_tokens` used for `global_bs` calculation comes from this parameter when
   `cudagraph_capture_sizes` is set.
3. The `mc2_tokens_capacity` in `ascend_forward_context.py:203` which controls memory
   allocation for MC2 (multi-core communication) operations.
4. The `decode_cudagraph_max_bs` in attention backends (gdn_attn.py:109, flashinfer.py:591)
   which caps the maximum batch size for full-cudagraph decode wrappers.
A larger value captures more graph sizes, improving throughput for variable batch sizes but increasing startup time and memory consumption. A smaller value reduces startup overhead and memory but may cause more graph misses (falling back to eager execution), hurting throughput. On Ascend, the 512 cap is particularly important to avoid excessive graph capture time and memory pressure on NPU.

legacy_profiles.name: --max-long-partial-prefills
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the maximum number of long prompts (those exceeding --long-prefill-token-threshold tokens) that can be partially prefilled concurrently during chunked prefill. When set lower than --max-num-partial-prefills, the scheduler reserves some concurrent prefill slots exclusively for short prompts, allowing them to bypass long prompts in the queue. This directly affects time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency for short requests under mixed-length workloads. On Ascend NPU, where chunked prefill is the default mode, this parameter shapes the prefill scheduling policy and thus impacts both latency fairness and overall throughput. The parameter is only active when --enable-chunked-prefill is True (default) and --max-num-partial-prefills > 1. No vllm-ascend specific override was found; the upstream vLLM behavior applies directly on Ascend.

legacy_profiles.name: --max-lora-rank
legacy_profiles.valid_choices: positive integer (typically 1-256, constrained by model architecture)
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the maximum rank of LoRA adapters that can be loaded. It directly determines the size of pre-allocated LoRA weight buffers in GPU/NPU memory. In vllm-ascend, the value also triggers a critical code path selection in PunicaWrapperNPU (vllm_ascend/lora/punica_npu.py:26): when max_lora_rank >= 128 or on AscendDeviceType._310P, the system falls back to PyTorch-native LoRA ops (bgmv_expand/shrink from vllm.lora.ops.torch_ops) instead of using the optimized vllm-ascend custom ops (vllm_ascend.lora.lora_ops). This fallback can significantly impact throughput and latency because the custom Ascend ops are tuned for NPU execution, while the PyTorch fallback may not leverage NPU-specific optimizations. Additionally, max_lora_rank affects the shape of all pre-allocated LoRA weight tensors (lora_a_stacked, lora_b_stacked) in every LoRA-enabled linear layer, MoE layer, and column-parallel layer — memory consumption scales linearly with this value. The parameter is also used in the computation graph hash (vllm/config/lora.py:88), meaning changes to it will invalidate cached compilation artifacts.

legacy_profiles.name: --max-loras
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: --max-loras controls the maximum number of distinct LoRA adapters that can be active in a single batch. This parameter directly affects throughput and latency because it acts as a hard scheduling constraint: "when the number of distinct" LoRA adapters in the running batch reaches max_loras, the scheduler skips all waiting requests that require a different LoRA adapter, even if token budget and sequence capacity remain available. This is enforced across ALL Ascend scheduler variants (balance_schedule, recompute_scheduler, dynamic_batch, profiling_chunk) via the same pattern: after recording scheduled_loras from running requests, the scheduler checks `len(scheduled_loras) == self.lora_config.max_loras` and skips requests whose lora_int_id is not already in the set. Additionally, max_loras affects CUDA graph capture: when cudagraph_specialize_lora is enabled, separate graphs are captured for powers of 2 up to max_loras, and when specialization is disabled, graphs are captured with max_loras + 1 active adapters. On Ascend NPU, the v1 worker's model_runner_v1.py uses max_loras as the num_active_loras for dummy runs (line 3297), which affects graph dispatch and memory allocation. Higher max_loras increases the number of CUDA graph variants captured, consuming more NPU memory and increasing capture time, but allows more LoRA diversity per batch, improving throughput in multi-tenant LoRA serving scenarios. Setting max_loras too low causes scheduler head-of-line blocking where requests with different LoRA adapters starve.

legacy_profiles.name: --max-model-len
legacy_profiles.valid_choices: integer >= -1; supports human-readable suffixes (k/m/g/K/M/G); -1 or 'auto' for automatic derivation
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
--max-model-len defines the maximum context length (prompt + output tokens) for a single request. On Ascend NPU, this parameter has a direct and multi-faceted performance impact:
1. **KV cache memory allocation**: The KV cache size is proportional to max_model_len.
   In vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_kv_cache_interface.py:188, max_model_len is used
   to compute max_memory_usage_bytes for each KV cache group. When decode context parallelism
   (DCP) or prefill context parallelism (PCP) is enabled (dcp_world_size * pcp_world_size > 1),
   the effective per-rank max_model_len is divided by the total CP world size, reducing
   per-device memory pressure. A larger max_model_len consumes more HBM for KV cache,
   leaving less memory for model weights and activations, potentially causing OOM.

2. **Block table sizing**: In vllm_ascend/worker/block_table.py:278-305, max_model_len
   determines max_num_blocks_per_req (cdiv(max_model_len, block_size * total_cp_world_size)).
   This directly controls the size of the block table tensor allocated per request,
   affecting both memory usage and the efficiency of slot mapping operations.

3. **Scheduling constraints**: In vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py:138,
   max_model_len acts as a hard upper bound during scheduling — num_new_tokens is clamped
   to max_model_len - 1 - request.num_computed_tokens. This prevents scheduling tokens
   beyond the model's capacity and ensures spec decoding does not exceed position limits.

4. **Mamba block size fallback**: In vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_mamba_config.py:116,
   when prefix caching is disabled and mamba_cache_mode is not "align", mamba_block_size
   falls back to max_model_len, meaning the entire sequence is treated as a single block.
   This can significantly affect memory efficiency for hybrid Mamba models.

5. **Throughput vs. memory tradeoff**: A larger max_model_len allows longer sequences
   but reduces the number of concurrent requests that can fit in KV cache, lowering
   throughput. Conversely, a smaller value increases concurrency but may cause requests
   to be rejected if they exceed the limit. The vllm-ascend documentation recommends
   reducing --max-model-len (along with --max-num-seqs) as the first troubleshooting
   step for OOM or unstable startup.

legacy_profiles.name: --max-num-batched-tokens
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter controls the maximum number of tokens (prefill + decode) that the scheduler can batch into a single model forward pass. It directly governs the compute intensity of each iteration and the peak activation memory footprint.
On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend applies several critical overrides and constraints beyond upstream vLLM:
1. **v1 worker padding (vllm_ascend/worker/model_runner_v1.py:261-293):** In the v1 worker,
   max_num_batched_tokens is temporarily increased by `pcp_size * 2 * max_num_seqs` during
   parent class initialization to allocate larger internal buffers for context-parallel padding,
   then restored afterward. This means the actual scheduling limit is unchanged, but internal
   buffer allocation accounts for PCP overhead.

2. **FLASHCOMM1 divisibility constraint (vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py:121-130):** When
   FLASHCOMM1 is enabled and prefill_context_parallel_size > 1, max_num_batched_tokens is
   silently rounded up to be divisible by `tp_size * pcp_size`. Non-divisible values are
   adjusted with a warning. This is required for correct communication pattern alignment.

3. **Profiling chunk interaction (vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py:57-67):** When
   profiling_chunk_config is enabled, if max_num_batched_tokens is smaller than the configured
   min_chunk, min_chunk is clamped down to max_num_batched_tokens to avoid silent ignoring.

4. **KV cache coordinator (vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_kv_cache_coordinator.py:56-68):**
   max_num_batched_tokens is passed to the KV cache coordinator and used as a recycling-aware
   admission cap. When unset (None), it falls back to max_model_len.

5. **Block table allocation (vllm_ascend/worker/block_table.py:92):** The slot_mapping buffer
   size is `max_num_batched_tokens + 2 * pcp_world_size * max_num_reqs`, directly coupling
   this parameter to device memory allocation.

6. **GPU memory profiling (documented in docs):** During warm-up profiling, vLLM records peak
   GPU memory usage with an input size of max_num_batched_tokens. The available KV cache is
   computed as `gpu_memory_utilization * HBM - peak_memory`. Larger values increase peak
   activation memory, reducing KV cache capacity and potentially causing OOM.

Larger values reduce scheduling overhead and improve throughput by batching more tokens per iteration, but increase activation memory pressure and may cause OOM. Smaller values reduce memory usage but increase the number of iterations needed for long prefill sequences (due to chunked prefill splitting).

legacy_profiles.name: --max-num-partial-prefills
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend silently overrides this parameter to 1 regardless of user input (vllm_ascend/platform.py:985-990). The override is unconditional — any non-default value triggers a warning and is reset to 1. This means concurrent partial prefills are effectively disabled on Ascend hardware. The parameter controls how many sequences can be partially prefilled in a single scheduler step when chunked prefill is enabled. On GPU platforms, increasing this value allows the scheduler to interleave multiple long prompts, improving latency fairness and throughput under mixed-length workloads. On Ascend, the override neutralizes this optimization, so the parameter has no runtime effect beyond the warning message. The performance impact is classified as "low" because the parameter is forcibly pinned to 1 on Ascend — users cannot change it, and the default behavior (single partial prefill) is the only behavior available.

legacy_profiles.name: --max-num-seqs
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter controls the maximum number of concurrent sequences (requests) the scheduler can process in a single iteration. It directly bounds batch size, which is the primary lever for throughput on Ascend NPU.
On Ascend, the impact is amplified by several vllm-ascend mechanisms:
1. **CUDA Graph capture size**: vllm-ascend overrides the default
   `max_cudagraph_capture_size` to `min(max_num_seqs * decode_query_len, 512)`
   (vllm_ascend/platform.py:211). This means `--max-num-seqs` directly
   determines how many CUDA graph sizes are captured, affecting startup time
   and memory usage. The upstream vLLM default multiplies by 2; Ascend removes
   this multiplier to reduce memory pressure.

2. **Buffer allocation**: Multiple Ascend attention backends allocate tensors
   sized by `max_num_seqs`:
   - "`start_pos_prefill` and `start_pos_decode` tensors in DSA metadata builder"
     (vllm_ascend/attention/dsa_v1.py:421-422)
   - "`actual_seq_lengths_query` in SFA metadata builder"
     (vllm_ascend/attention/sfa_v1.py:208-209)
   - "`local_query_start_loc` and `local_seq_lens` in DSA CP builder"
     (vllm_ascend/attention/context_parallel/dsa_cp.py:200-209)
   - "Slot mapping buffer padding in SFA CP:"
     `max_num_batched_tokens + 2 * pcp_size * max_num_seqs`
     (vllm_ascend/attention/context_parallel/sfa_cp.py:54)

3. **PCP padding**: In the v1 model runner, `max_num_batched_tokens` is
   temporarily increased by `pcp_size * 2 * max_num_seqs` to accommodate
   context-parallel padding (vllm_ascend/worker/model_runner_v1.py:259).

4. **Speculative decoding**: `max_num_seqs` multiplies with
   `max_num_new_slots_for_drafting` to reserve token budget for draft slots
   (vllm/config/vllm.py:1437). Setting it too high with speculative decoding
   can cause `max_num_scheduled_tokens <= 0` errors.

5. **Mamba models**: Each decode sequence requires one Mamba cache block.
   If `max_num_seqs > num_blocks`, CUDA graph capture raises a ValueError
   (vllm/config/compilation.py:1435-1441).

Higher values increase maximum throughput but consume more NPU memory for buffers and KV cache. Lower values reduce memory pressure and startup time but cap concurrency.

legacy_profiles.name: --max-parallel-loading-workers
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls the maximum number of worker processes that load model weights in parallel during model initialization. When using tensor parallelism with large models, loading all shards simultaneously can cause RAM OOM on the host because each worker loads its full weight shard into CPU memory before transferring to NPU. By limiting parallel loading workers, weights are loaded sequentially in batches, reducing peak host RAM usage at the cost of slower model loading time. This parameter does not affect runtime inference throughput or latency — it only impacts initialization memory and startup time. On Ascend NPU, the same host RAM pressure exists, and since Ascend servers often have large numbers of NPUs per node (e.g., 8-card Atlas 800T A2), the default of unlimited parallel loading can cause OOM during model loading for large models like Llama-70B or DeepSeek-V2.

legacy_profiles.name: --mm-encoder-attn-dtype
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls whether the ViT (Vision Transformer) encoder attention layers use FP8 quantization. When set to "fp8", it enables the FlashInfer cuDNN FP8 prefill attention backend, which quantizes Q/K/V tensors to FP8 before the attention computation. This reduces memory bandwidth pressure and speeds up attention computation on hardware with native FP8 support. On Ascend NPU, the critical constraint is that the FlashInfer cuDNN backend is required — this backend is CUDA-specific and NOT available on Ascend. The code in vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mm_encoder_attention.py:396 explicitly checks `is_flashinfer_cudnn_fp8_prefill_attn_supported()` and raises a ValueError if the platform does not support it. Since Ascend NPU does not have cuDNN or FlashInfer cuDNN backend, setting this parameter to "fp8" on Ascend will cause a runtime error. When left as null (default), the encoder attention uses the standard dtype (typically bfloat16 or float16), which is the only viable path on Ascend. The parameter has no Ascend-specific override in vllm-ascend, meaning the upstream behavior applies directly — and it is incompatible with Ascend hardware.

legacy_profiles.name: --mm-encoder-fp8-scale-save-margin
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter is a safety multiplier applied to dynamically calibrated FP8 scales when they are auto-saved via `mm_encoder_fp8_scale_save_path`. It does NOT affect runtime inference directly — it only modifies the scale values written to the saved JSON file. The saved file can then be used as `mm_encoder_fp8_scale_path` in subsequent runs to enable static FP8 scaling for the ViT encoder attention. A larger margin produces more conservative (smaller) scales, reducing the risk of FP8 overflow on inputs with larger activations than the calibration set, at the cost of slightly reduced numerical precision. The parameter is read once during model initialization (in `MMEncoderAttention.__init__`, line 431 of mm_encoder_attention.py) and stored in a module-level global `_fp8_scale_save_margin`. It is consumed during the forward pass when the amax history buffer wraps and scales are saved (in `_maybe_save_fp8_scales`). On Ascend NPU, the FP8 attention backend for ViT encoders follows the same vLLM upstream path — there is no vllm-ascend override for this parameter. The performance impact is indirect: it affects the quality of statically-scaled FP8 inference in subsequent runs, which can influence throughput and latency if the saved scales cause numerical issues requiring fallback or recomputation.

legacy_profiles.name: --mm-encoder-only
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled, this flag causes vLLM to skip the entire language model (LLM) component and run only the multimodal encoder. This is designed for disaggregated serving architectures where the encoder and decoder run on separate processes. On Ascend NPU, the performance impact is dramatic: "the language model (which dominates both compute" and memory) is completely bypassed. In v1 worker, the dummy run for CUDA graph capture returns immediately without executing any LM operations (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:5373-5376), and the dummy sampler run also short-circuits (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:5711-5713). During model initialization, language model layers are replaced with StageMissingLayer placeholders via no_init_weights context manager (vllm/model_executor/models/interfaces.py:241-242), which means those layers are never materialized on the NPU. This drastically reduces NPU memory consumption and eliminates all LM computation, making the process a pure encoder that only handles multimodal feature extraction. The encoder output is typically transferred to a separate decoder process via IPC or network. This parameter is mutually exclusive with normal end-to-end inference — it fundamentally changes the process role from full model server to encoder-only server.

legacy_profiles.name: --mm-encoder-tp-mode
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls how the multi-modal encoder (vision tower) leverages tensor parallelism (TP). In "weights" mode, encoder layer weights are sharded across TP ranks — each rank holds a portion of the weights and computes a partial result, requiring all-reduce communication per layer. This is the standard TP behavior and works with all models. In "data" mode, each TP rank holds a full copy of the encoder weights and processes a different subset of the input batch (batch-level data parallelism within the encoder). This eliminates encoder-internal all-reduce communication entirely, trading increased per-rank memory (full weight replicas) for higher encoder throughput and lower latency. The mode is checked at runtime in vllm/v1/worker/encoder_cudagraph.py:108 where `use_dp` is set to True only when mode is "data" AND tensor_parallel_size > 1. Individual models declare support via the `supports_encoder_tp_data` class attribute (e.g., dots_ocr.py:644, eagle2_5_vl.py:139). If a model does not support "data" mode, it silently falls back to "weights" behavior per the docstring at multimodal.py:156-157. On Ascend NPU, the "data" mode is particularly beneficial because it avoids HCCL all-reduce overhead in the encoder, which can be significant for vision transformers with many small layers. The vllm-ascend documentation explicitly recommends "data" mode for multimodal inference workloads (Kimi-K2.5.md:182).

legacy_profiles.name: --mm-processor-cache-gb
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls the size of the LRU cache that stores preprocessed multimodal inputs (images, videos, audio) to avoid redundant processing across requests. The cache is duplicated for each API server process and each engine core process, so total memory consumption is `mm_processor_cache_gb * (api_server_count + data_parallel_size)`. On Ascend NPU, this cache resides in CPU memory (not NPU HBM), but it still competes with other CPU-side allocations and can affect overall system memory pressure. When set to 0, the cache is disabled entirely, forcing every multimodal input to be reprocessed from scratch — this increases latency for repeated inputs but eliminates the CPU memory overhead. The vllm-ascend documentation explicitly notes that `--mm-processor-cache-gb 0` must be set to disable the cache when using cross-process caching in EPD disaggregation scenarios, as the two caching mechanisms conflict.

legacy_profiles.name: --mm-processor-cache-type
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
Controls the caching strategy for multi-modal preprocessor/mapper outputs. Two modes exist: 1. `lru` (default): Uses a mirrored LRU cache per process. Each API server
   and engine core process maintains its own copy of cached multi-modal
   tensors, consuming `mm_processor_cache_gb` memory per process. Total
   memory usage = `mm_processor_cache_gb * (api_server_count + data_parallel_size)`.
2. `shm`: Uses a shared memory FIFO cache backed by a POSIX shared memory
   buffer. All processes share a single cache instance, reducing total memory
   consumption. However, `shm` requires IPC support: it only activates when
   `_api_process_count == 1` AND (`data_parallel_size == 1` OR
   `data_parallel_external_lb` is True). If IPC is unsupported, the cache
   falls back to `processor_only` mode (no cross-process sharing). The `shm`
   mode also requires a `shared_worker_lock` to be passed from the executor;
   if missing, vLLM raises a ValueError. On Ascend NPU, multi-modal models
   (e.g., Qwen2-VL, InternVL) benefit from `shm` when running with multiple
   workers, as it avoids redundant NPU memory allocations for identical
   preprocessed tensors. The `shm` cache has a per-object size limit
   controlled by `--mm-shm-cache-max-object-size-mb` (default 128 MiB).

usage_locations.context: `_get_cache_type()` returns `mm_processor_cache_type` to determine which cache implementation to instantiate.
`processor_cache_from_config()` dispatches to `MultiModalProcessorSenderCache` for `lru`, `ShmObjectStoreSenderCache` for `shm`, or `MultiModalProcessorOnlyCache` for `processor_only` fallback.
Worker initialization checks if `mm_processor_cache_type == "shm"` and requires `shared_worker_lock`; raises ValueError if missing.
`VLLM_OBJECT_STORAGE_SHM_BUFFER_NAME` env var is only effective when `mm_processor_cache_type == "shm"`.

related_parameters.name: --mm-processor-cache-gb
related_parameters.relation: Sets the cache size in GiB. Total memory consumption scales with this value multiplied by process count for `lru` mode; shared across processes for `shm` mode.

related_parameters.name: --mm-shm-cache-max-object-size-mb
related_parameters.relation: Only effective when `--mm-processor-cache-type shm`. Limits the maximum size of individual objects stored in the shared memory cache.

related_parameters.name: VLLM_OBJECT_STORAGE_SHM_BUFFER_NAME
related_parameters.relation: Environment variable that names the shared memory buffer; only used when `--mm-processor-cache-type shm`.

constraints: --mm-shm-cache-max-object-size-mb must only be set when --mm-processor-cache-type is 'shm'; otherwise vLLM raises a ValueError.

The 'shm' cache type requires IPC support: _api_process_count must be 1 and either data_parallel_size must be 1 or data_parallel_external_lb must be True; otherwise the cache falls back to 'processor_only' mode.
When --mm-processor-cache-type is 'shm', the executor must provide a shared_worker_lock; if missing, vLLM raises a ValueError.

tuning_advice.summary: Use `shm` on Ascend NPU for multi-modal models with multiple workers to reduce redundant memory consumption; fall back to `lru` when IPC is unavailable or for single-process deployments.

suggested_values.scenario: Multi-modal model (e.g., Qwen2-VL) with data_parallel_size > 1 or multiple API server processes on Ascend NPU.
suggested_values.reason: Shared memory cache avoids duplicating preprocessed multi-modal tensors across processes, reducing total NPU host/device memory pressure and improving throughput by eliminating redundant preprocessing.

suggested_values.scenario: Single-process deployment or when IPC is unavailable (e.g., _api_process_count > 1 without external load balancing).
suggested_values.reason: The `shm` cache requires IPC support; when unavailable, vLLM automatically falls back to `processor_only` mode, which provides no cross-request caching benefit. `lru` at least provides per-process caching.

caveats: On Ascend NPU, multi-modal preprocessing tensors can be large (hundreds of MiB for high-resolution images/videos). Duplicating these across workers with `lru` can quickly exhaust host memory, especially on systems with limited RAM (e.g., Atlas 800T A2 with 64 GB host memory).
The `shm` cache uses POSIX shared memory (`/dev/shm`). Ensure sufficient space in `/dev/shm` (typically half of host RAM by default on Linux). Monitor with `df -h /dev/shm`.
When `shm` is active but IPC conditions are not met, the cache silently degrades to `processor_only` mode with no cross-request caching — this can cause a performance regression compared to `lru`.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: For multi-modal models on Ascend NPU with multiple workers, prefer `--mm-processor-cache-type shm` to share preprocessed tensors and reduce memory duplication.

legacy_profiles.name: --mm-processor-kwargs
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter forwards keyword arguments to the HuggingFace AutoProcessor for multi-modal data (e.g., image/video processor). The specific keys and their effects depend entirely on the model being served. For vision-language models like Qwen3-VL, common overrides include `min_pixels`, `max_pixels`, and `fps`, which directly control image resolution and video frame sampling rate.
Performance mechanism: 1. **Throughput**: Higher `max_pixels` increases the number of vision tokens per image, which
   increases the sequence length processed by the language model. This directly reduces throughput
   (tokens/sec) because more compute is spent per image. Conversely, lower `max_pixels` reduces
   vision tokens and improves throughput at the cost of visual detail.
2. **Memory**: Larger images (higher pixel limits) produce more vision tokens, consuming more
   KV cache memory. On Ascend NPU with limited HBM, this can cause OOM if `max_pixels` is set
   too high relative to `max_model_len` and `gpu_memory_utilization`.
3. **Latency**: Time-to-first-token (TTFT) increases with more vision tokens because the
   vision encoder must process larger images and the language model must prefill more tokens.

The parameter is defined in `vllm/config/multimodal.py:114` as `mm_processor_kwargs: dict[str, object] | None = None` and is passed through `MultiModalConfig.merge_mm_processor_kwargs()` (line 326) which merges config-level kwargs with per-request inference kwargs. On Ascend, vllm-ascend does NOT override this parameter — it passes through unchanged. The Ascend test suite (e.g., `tests/e2e/conftest.py:1681`, `tests/e2e/pull_request/one_card/test_vlm.py:55`) uses typical values like `min_pixels=784`, `max_pixels=1280*28*28` (1003520), and `fps=1` for Qwen3-VL models, confirming these work on Ascend NPU.

suggested_values.reason: Lower fps reduces the number of sampled frames, decreasing total vision tokens for video inputs; combined with moderate max_pixels to keep memory usage manageable.

caveats: The `fps` key only affects video inputs; for image-only workloads it has no effect.
Setting `max_pixels` too low may cause the model to miss fine-grained visual details, degrading answer quality for tasks like OCR or document understanding.
On Ascend NPU, vision encoder execution may have different performance characteristics than GPU; test with representative images to find the optimal pixel limits for your hardware.

tuning_advice.quick_guide: For Ascend NPU, start with `min_pixels=784, max_pixels=501760` for Qwen3-VL to balance quality and memory; increase max_pixels only if visual detail is insufficient.

legacy_profiles.name: mm-shm-cache-max-object-size-mb
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter sets the maximum size (in MiB) for each individual object stored in the multi-modal processor's shared memory (SHM) cache. It is only effective when `--mm-processor-cache-type` is set to `"shm"`. The value is used to initialize `SingleWriterShmObjectStorage` with `max_object_size` (converted to bytes by multiplying by `MiB_bytes`), which controls the allocation of shared memory segments for cached multi-modal inputs. Objects larger than this limit cannot be stored in the SHM cache, forcing re-processing of those multi-modal inputs on subsequent requests. This can increase latency for requests with large multi-modal inputs (e.g., high-resolution images or long videos) and reduce cache hit rates, indirectly affecting throughput. On Ascend NPU, the multi-modal encoder runs on the host CPU or NPU depending on the model architecture; cache misses mean repeated encoder computation, which consumes NPU compute resources and PCIe bandwidth for data transfer. The parameter does not directly control KV-cache or model weight memory, so its overall performance impact is low compared to primary memory/parallelism parameters.

Receiver cache initialization: max_object_size = mm_shm_cache_max_object_size_mb * MiB_bytes

legacy_profiles.name: --mm-tensor-ipc
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
Controls the inter-process communication mechanism for transferring multimodal tensor data (e.g., image/video embeddings) between the API server process and the engine core worker processes. The two modes have distinct performance characteristics:
- "\"direct_rpc\" (default): Uses msgspec serialization over RPC. Tensors are"
  serialized to bytes, transmitted, then deserialized. This incurs CPU
  serialization overhead and memory copies, which can become a bottleneck
  for large multimodal inputs (high-resolution images, long videos).

- "\"torch_shm\": Uses torch.multiprocessing shared memory for zero-copy IPC."
  Tensors are placed in shared memory and the receiver reads them directly,
  eliminating serialization overhead. This is particularly beneficial for
  Ascend NPU deployments where multimodal models process large visual
  feature tensors — avoiding CPU serialization reduces both latency and
  CPU utilization, allowing the NPU to stay fed with data.

On Ascend NPU, the performance gain from "torch_shm" can be significant because: "(1) multimodal encoder outputs can be large tensors that are" expensive to serialize; (2) NPU inference is fast enough that CPU-side serialization becomes the bottleneck; (3) shared memory avoids extra CPU↔NPU data movement that serialization would require.
The parameter is read in vllm/v1/engine/core_client.py:551 and vllm/v1/engine/utils.py:1020 to decide whether to create a tensor_queue for shared memory IPC. When "torch_shm" is selected, a multiprocessing Queue is created and passed to TensorIpcSender for zero-copy transfers.

Creates multiprocessing Queue for shared memory IPC when mm_tensor_ipc is "torch_shm"

suggested_values.reason: Eliminates msgspec serialization overhead for large multimodal tensors, reducing end-to-end latency and CPU utilization. On Ascend NPU where inference is fast, CPU-side serialization can become the bottleneck; shared memory zero-copy keeps the NPU fed with minimal CPU intervention.

legacy_profiles.name: --model-impl
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter controls which model implementation backend is used for inference. On Ascend NPU, the choice directly affects performance because:
1. "vllm" uses vLLM's optimized model implementations, which include Ascend-specific
   kernel optimizations, custom attention backends, and NPU-aware memory management.
   These implementations are designed for high throughput and low latency on Ascend hardware.

2. "transformers" falls back to HuggingFace Transformers implementations, which lack
   Ascend-specific optimizations and may use generic PyTorch operations that are not
   optimized for the Da Vinci architecture. This typically results in significantly
   lower throughput and higher memory usage.

3. "auto" (default) attempts to use vLLM implementation first, falling back to
   Transformers only when no vLLM implementation exists. This is the safest choice
   but may silently degrade performance if a model lacks vLLM support.

4. "terratorch" is a specialized backend for geospatial models and is not relevant
   for most Ascend deployments.

The model resolution logic in vllm/model_executor/models/registry.py shows that when model_impl="vllm", the system strictly requires a vLLM implementation and will raise an error if none exists. When model_impl="auto", it gracefully falls back to Transformers with a warning about suboptimal performance.
On Ascend NPU, using "vllm" is strongly recommended because vllm-ascend provides Ascend-optimized implementations for many popular model architectures. Using "transformers" bypasses these optimizations entirely.

suggested_values.reason: Uses Ascend-optimized model implementations from vllm-ascend, providing the best throughput, lowest latency, and most efficient memory usage on NPU.

suggested_values.reason: Useful for isolating whether a performance issue is specific to the vLLM implementation. Not recommended for production due to significantly lower performance on Ascend NPU.

caveats: Using --model-impl transformers on Ascend NPU typically results in 2-5x lower throughput compared to vllm due to lack of Ascend-specific kernel optimizations.
When --model-impl auto silently falls back to Transformers, a warning is logged but the server starts successfully — always check startup logs for fallback warnings.
Some advanced vLLM features (speculative decoding, chunked prefill, prefix caching) may not work with Transformers backend, further reducing performance.
The vllm-ascend plugin does not override this parameter, but it provides Ascend-optimized implementations that are only used when model_impl is "vllm" or "auto" (with vLLM support).
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Set --model-impl vllm for best Ascend NPU performance; check startup logs for fallback warnings if using auto.

legacy_profiles.name: --moe-backend
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter selects the backend kernel implementation for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) expert computation. On Ascend NPU, the available backends are limited to those supported by the CANN/HCCL stack. The "auto" default delegates selection to vLLM's automatic backend resolution, which on Ascend typically falls back to "triton" or "triton_unfused" since GPU-specific backends (deep_gemm, cutlass, flashinfer_*, aiter) are not available on NPU. The parameter is consumed in FusedMoE layer construction (vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/layer.py:511) where it is passed to FusedMoEConfig.moe_backend, which then drives kernel selection in the MoE dispatch path. Since Ascend NPU lacks most of the listed backends, the effective choice is between "auto" (which resolves to a Triton-based path) and "triton"/"triton_unfused" for explicit control. The performance difference between these options on Ascend is minimal because they all ultimately rely on the same underlying CANN operators. No vllm-ascend override of this parameter was found in the provided context.

legacy_profiles.name: --num-gpu-blocks-override
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter directly overrides the profiled `num_gpu_blocks` in the KV cache configuration. When set to a non-None value, it replaces the automatically determined number of GPU KV cache blocks (which is calculated based on available GPU memory and `gpu_memory_utilization`) with a user-specified value. This affects:
1. **Memory allocation**: The KV cache is the primary consumer of GPU memory during inference.
   Setting this too high causes out-of-memory (OOM) errors; setting it too low wastes GPU memory
   and reduces the maximum batch size / sequence length that can be served.

2. **Throughput and latency**: The number of KV cache blocks determines how many tokens can be
   stored simultaneously. Fewer blocks mean the scheduler must evict or preempt requests more
   aggressively, reducing throughput and increasing latency. More blocks allow larger batches
   and longer sequences, improving throughput but potentially increasing per-token latency due
   to larger memory footprint.

3. **Auto-fit behavior**: In v1, when `original_max_model_len` is -1 (auto), the system
   automatically determines the maximum model length that fits in available GPU memory. The
   override decouples the cache size from profiled `available_memory`, and the code at
   `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:1984-2003` adjusts `available_memory` to reflect the
   override so that auto-fit, admission checks, and per-worker config builders all plan
   against the same effective capacity.

4. **CUDA graph profiling**: During CUDA graph capture, the system temporarily overrides
   `num_gpu_blocks_override` to allocate a minimal KV cache (`max_cudagraph_capture_size`
   blocks) for profiling purposes, then restores the original value. This is visible at
   `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:5973-5979`.

On Ascend NPU, the KV cache is allocated in NPU HBM (High Bandwidth Memory). The same override mechanism applies, but the practical effect depends on the available NPU memory and the memory overhead of the Ascend CANN runtime. vllm-ascend does not override or modify this parameter's behavior, but the effective number of blocks that can be allocated is constrained by NPU HBM capacity, which may differ from GPU VRAM capacity for the same model.
The parameter is explicitly excluded from the computation graph hash (`vllm/config/cache.py:194`), meaning changing it does not trigger recompilation.

legacy_profiles.name: --numa-bind
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: On Ascend NPU, --numa-bind is silently overridden by vllm-ascend (vllm_ascend/platform.py:1092). When set to true, vllm-ascend resets it to false and instead sets additional_config={"enable_cpu_binding": true}, which triggers Ascend-native CPU-core binding based on NPU topology rather than GPU-to-NUMA detection. The actual performance effect comes from the Ascend-native CPU binding mechanism, not from the upstream NUMA binding code path. The upstream NUMA binding (vllm/utils/numa_utils.py) relies on numactl and GPU-to-NUMA topology detection, neither of which is applicable to Ascend NPUs. The Ascend-native replacement performs automatic topo-affinity CPU binding, which can reduce cross-socket memory access latency and improve tail latency stability, but the magnitude of improvement is typically modest (low single-digit percentage) on Ascend hardware.

legacy_profiles.name: --offload-backend
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter selects the backend for model weight offloading from GPU/NPU memory to CPU memory. On Ascend NPU, weight offloading is critical for deploying large models that exceed device HBM capacity. The three backends have fundamentally different performance profiles: - "\"auto\": Automatically selects prefetch if --offload-group-size > 0, UVA if --cpu-offload-gb > 0,"
  otherwise disables offloading entirely (NoopOffloader). This is the default and safest choice.
- "\"uva\": Uses Unified Virtual Addressing for zero-copy access to CPU memory. On Ascend NPU,"
  UVA offloading relies on the host-to-device DMA engine. Each layer access triggers a
  synchronous or asynchronous copy from CPU to NPU, which can severely impact throughput
  if the model has many layers and the PCIe/NPU-link bandwidth is insufficient.
- "\"prefetch\": Uses async prefetch with group-based layer offloading. Layers are divided into"
  groups (controlled by --offload-group-size), and a subset (--offload-num-in-group) is kept
  on NPU while the rest reside on CPU. The prefetch step (--offload-prefetch-step) determines
  how many layers ahead to prefetch. This is generally more throughput-friendly than UVA
  because it overlaps computation with data transfer, but requires careful tuning of group
  parameters to avoid stalls.

The selection logic in create_offloader() (vllm/model_executor/offloader/base.py:129-162) shows that when backend="auto" and neither offload_group_size nor cpu_offload_gb is set, a NoopOffloader is returned — meaning no offloading occurs and all weights stay on NPU. This is the highest-performance option when model fits in HBM.
Note: "vllm-ascend does NOT override or modify this parameter's behavior. The offloading" mechanism is upstream vLLM code and works identically on Ascend NPU as on GPU, subject to the NPU's DMA and PCIe bandwidth characteristics.

legacy_profiles.name: --offload-group-size
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the prefetch-based model weight offloading strategy. When set to a positive integer N, it groups every N consecutive transformer layers together and offloads the last `offload_num_in_group` layers of each group to CPU memory. This reduces GPU memory usage at the cost of CPU-GPU data transfer during inference. Unlike the simpler `cpu_offload_gb` (UVA-based) approach, this uses explicit async prefetching to hide transfer latency by overlapping H2D copies with computation. On Ascend NPU, the memory savings are critical for deploying large models within the limited HBM of NPU cards, but the PCIe/NPU interconnect bandwidth and the effectiveness of async prefetch overlap will determine the actual throughput impact. Setting this to a value > 0 also implicitly selects the "prefetch" offload backend when `offload_backend` is "auto" (see vllm/model_executor/offloader/base.py:141).

legacy_profiles.valid_choices: any set of parameter name segments (strings)
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls which model parameters are offloaded to CPU memory when using the prefetch-based offloading backend (--offload-group-size > 0). It acts as a whitelist filter: "only parameters whose names contain one of" the specified segments are offloaded. When empty (default), ALL parameters of each offloaded layer are offloaded. When non-empty, only matching parameters are offloaded, reducing CPU-GPU transfer volume and GPU memory usage for offload buffers. The matching logic in vllm/model_executor/offloader/prefetch.py:181-186 uses segment matching: `f".{p}." in f".{name}."` — so "w13_weight" matches "mlp.experts.w13_weight" but not "mlp.experts.w13_weight_scale". This allows fine-grained control over which weight tensors (e.g., only MLP weights, only MoE expert weights) are offloaded, directly affecting: (1) GPU memory saved by offloading, (2) CPU-GPU transfer bandwidth consumption, and (3) inference latency due to H2D transfer overhead. On Ascend NPU, the same mechanism applies — the offloader uses PyTorch streams for async H2D, which maps to HCCL/CANN memory operations. Selective offloading is particularly important for Ascend NPUs with limited HBM capacity (e.g., 64GB on Atlas 800T A2) where offloading only the largest parameter groups (like MoE expert weights) can make large models fit while minimizing the performance penalty.

legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the lookahead distance for asynchronous CPU-to-GPU layer prefetching in the prefetch offloading backend. When --offload-group-size > 0 (or --offload-backend prefetch), the PrefetchOffloader divides model layers into groups and offloads the last offload_num_in_group layers of each group to CPU memory. During inference, before executing layer i, the offloader initiates an async H2D transfer for layer i + offload_prefetch_step, overlapping the transfer with computation of the current layer. A higher value increases the overlap window, potentially hiding more CPU-GPU transfer latency and improving throughput. However, each prefetched layer occupies GPU memory, so higher values increase peak GPU memory usage. The tradeoff is latency hiding vs. memory consumption. On Ascend NPU, the same mechanism applies — the parameter is passed through to the upstream PrefetchOffloader without vllm-ascend override. The parameter has no effect when offload_group_size=0 (prefetch offloading disabled).

It is passed through to the model configuration and used by attention backends during initialization. The actual performance impact depends on whether the Ascend attention backend (e.g., torch_npu-based FlashAttention) supports the chosen dtype natively — if not, it may fall back to a slower generic implementation or cause errors.

legacy_profiles.name: --performance-mode
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter sets the `PerformanceMode` enum on `VllmConfig`, which is a hint consumed by the vLLM engine to select between latency-optimized and throughput-optimized code paths. The docstring in vllm/config/vllm.py:346-351 states that 'interactivity' favors low end-to-end per-request latency at small batch sizes (fine-grained CUDA graphs, latency-oriented kernels), while 'throughput' favors aggregate tokens/sec at high concurrency (larger CUDA graphs, more aggressive batching, throughput-oriented kernels). On Ascend NPU, CUDA graphs are not used (the platform uses CANN graph compilation via torch_npu instead), so the CUDA-graph-related tuning hints have no direct effect. However, the mode value is still read by the scheduler and model runner to adjust batching aggressiveness and kernel selection, which can indirectly influence Ascend runtime behavior. The vllm-ascend plugin does NOT override or intercept this parameter — it passes through to the upstream VllmConfig unchanged. The impact on Ascend is therefore limited to the upstream code paths that check `performance_mode` and adjust scheduling or kernel dispatch accordingly.

legacy_profiles.name: --pipeline-parallel-size
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
Pipeline parallelism splits model layers across multiple Ascend NPUs, enabling models that exceed single-device memory to run. On Ascend, this parameter directly controls:
1) **Memory distribution**: Each pipeline stage holds only a subset of layers, reducing per-device memory pressure proportionally to pp_size. This is the primary mechanism for running large models on Ascend NPUs with limited HBM.
2) **Throughput via pipelining**: Multiple micro-batches can be in-flight simultaneously across pipeline stages, improving device utilization. The Ascend-specific dynamic chunked pipeline parallel feature (profiling_chunk_config) requires pp_size > 1 and dynamically adjusts chunk sizes based on profiling data to optimize pipeline bubble reduction.
3) **Communication overhead**: Pipeline parallelism introduces point-to-point communication between stages via HCCL. The communication volume is proportional to hidden_size × num_microbatches, which can become a bottleneck if stages are imbalanced or chunk sizes are suboptimal.
4) **Ascend-specific constraints**: vllm-ascend enforces that xlite graph mode is incompatible with pp_size > 1 (raises RuntimeError). The profiling_chunk_config feature requires pp_size > 1 (raises ValueError otherwise). MoE communication type selection uses pp_size in world_size_across_dp // pp_size calculation.
5) **KV transfer impact**: Mooncake connectors use pp_size for device ID calculation and port assignment in disaggregated prefill-decode setups.
6) **Model compatibility**: Only models implementing the SupportsPP interface can use pipeline parallelism; otherwise a NotImplementedError is raised.

legacy_profiles.name: --prefill-context-parallel-size
legacy_profiles.valid_choices: positive integer; must divide tensor_parallel_size on Ascend
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
Controls the number of prefill context parallel (PCP) groups, which shard the KV cache along the sequence dimension during prefill to reduce per-device memory footprint and enable long-context inference. On Ascend NPU, PCP interacts with multiple subsystems:
1. **World size calculation** (vllm/config/parallel.py:765): world_size = pp_size × tp_size × pcp_size.
   Increasing PCP multiplies the total number of required NPU devices.

2. **KV cache memory** (vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_kv_cache_interface.py:190-194):
   When dcp × pcp > 1, max_model_len is divided by dcp × pcp, proportionally reducing
   per-device KV cache memory usage. This is the primary mechanism enabling long sequences.

3. **Block size alignment** (vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_kv_cache_utils.py:40-56):
   Ascend patches the upstream block size resolver to support CP with multiple KV cache
   groups. scheduler_block_size = lcm(group_block_sizes) × dcp × pcp, ensuring proper
   alignment for Ascend's MLA and SWA-MLA layers.

4. **FLASHCOMM1 constraint** (vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py:116-130): When FLASHCOMM1 is
   enabled and pcp > 1, max_num_batched_tokens is automatically adjusted to be divisible
   by tp_size × pcp_size to satisfy communication alignment requirements.

5. **V1 worker padding** (vllm_ascend/worker/model_runner_v1.py:258-261): The V1 model
   runner adds pcp_size × 2 × max_num_seqs padding tokens to max_num_batched_tokens to
   accommodate PCP communication buffers.

6. **V2 worker unsupported** (vllm_ascend/worker/v2/model_runner.py:68-69): The Ascend V2
   model runner explicitly raises NotImplementedError when pcp > 1, meaning PCP only works
   with the V1 worker on Ascend.

7. **P/D disaggregation** (vllm_ascend/platform.py:615-625): When KV transfer is configured
   and cp_size > 1, cp_kv_cache_interleave_size must equal block_size.

Performance-wise, PCP reduces per-device KV cache memory (enabling longer contexts or larger batch sizes) at the cost of additional all-to-all communication during prefill attention, which increases prefill latency. The tradeoff is favorable for long-context workloads where a single device cannot hold the full KV cache.

The hash is computed on every request's token blocks during scheduling (vllm/v1/engine/core.py:205). A faster hash algorithm (xxhash) reduces CPU overhead in the scheduling loop, which can marginally improve throughput and reduce scheduling latency under high request rates. However, the hash computation is typically a tiny fraction of overall inference time, so the performance impact is low. The parameter does not affect NPU-specific execution paths — it is purely a CPU-side scheduling optimization.

legacy_profiles.name: --quantization
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
The --quantization parameter determines the weight quantization method applied to the model. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend overrides the upstream vLLM supported_quantization list to only include "ascend", "compressed-tensors", "fp8", and "deepseek_v4_fp8" (vllm_ascend/platform.py:118-123). The "ascend" quantization method is dynamically injected into the CLI parser choices at runtime (vllm_ascend/platform.py:160-167) so users can pass --quantization ascend.
Performance impact is high because: 1. Weight quantization directly reduces model memory footprint, enabling larger batch sizes
   and higher throughput on memory-constrained NPU devices.
2. Quantized weights reduce memory bandwidth pressure during GEMM operations, which is
   critical for decode-heavy workloads where GEMM is memory-bound.
3. The "ascend" quantization method triggers Ascend-specific quantization paths
   (AscendCompressedTensorsConfig, AscendFp8Config, AscendModelSlimConfig) that leverage
   CANN-optimized kernels for quantized computation.
4. For MiniMax-M2 fp8 checkpoints on NPU, vllm-ascend patches the quantization verification
   to disable fp8 quantization and load dequantized bf16 weights instead
   (vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_minimax_m2_config.py:17-18, 65-71), which affects
   memory usage and precision.
5. The quantization method affects KV cache quantization compatibility — all attention layers
   in the same KV cache group must use the same quantization method
   (vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_kv_cache_interface.py:169).
6. FP8 quantization is not supported by the FA3 (Flash Attention 3) backend on NPU
   (documentation: flash_attention.md:42, 139), so using fp8 quantization forces fallback
   to the default FIA backend, impacting attention computation performance.

legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the size of the ThreadPoolExecutor used by the renderer (vllm/renderers/base.py:88-89). The thread pool handles async tokenization, chat template rendering, and multimodal preprocessing. Increasing the number of workers allows concurrent processing of multiple requests' tokenization and multimodal preprocessing, which can improve throughput under high concurrency by preventing the renderer from becoming a bottleneck. However, each worker may hold its own copy of the tokenizer (vllm/renderers/hf.py:809 configures the tokenizer's internal thread pool as renderer_num_workers + 1), increasing memory usage. On Ascend NPU, where host CPU memory may be more constrained relative to GPU memory, excessive workers could cause CPU memory pressure. The parameter has a hard constraint: it cannot be > 1 when multimodal processor cache is enabled (vllm/config/model.py:676-686), as the cache is not thread-safe.

legacy_profiles.name: --safetensors-load-strategy
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls how safetensors checkpoint files are read from disk during model loading. The strategy directly affects model initialization time (startup latency) and peak CPU RAM usage. On Ascend NPU, model loading is a critical phase because weights must be transferred from CPU to NPU device memory via the CANN runtime. The loading strategy determines whether weights are memory-mapped (lazy), fully read into CPU RAM (eager), or prefetched into the OS page cache (prefetch). For network filesystems (NFS, Lustre) commonly used in Ascend cluster deployments, the default None strategy auto-detects NFS and enables prefetching when the checkpoint fits within 90% of available RAM. The eager strategy avoids inefficient random reads on network storage at the cost of higher CPU RAM usage. The torchao strategy is automatically set when using torchao-quantized checkpoints. No vllm-ascend specific overrides were found for this parameter — it follows upstream vLLM behavior exactly.

legacy_profiles.name: --safetensors-prefetch-block-size
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the read block size (in bytes) used when prefetching safetensors checkpoint files into the OS page cache during model loading. It only takes effect when safetensors_load_strategy is "prefetch" (or when auto-detected for network filesystems like NFS/Lustre where the checkpoint fits in RAM). The prefetch is performed by worker threads that read the checkpoint files sequentially in blocks of this size, warming the OS page cache so that subsequent model weight loading sees lower I/O latency. Since this only affects the one-time model loading phase (not per-request inference), its impact on steady-state throughput and latency is negligible. However, a poorly chosen block size can slow down model startup time, especially on Ascend NPU systems where model weights must be loaded from host CPU memory to NPU device memory — faster host-side I/O reduces the overall initialization latency before the server is ready to serve requests.

legacy_profiles.name: --scheduler-cls
legacy_profiles.valid_choices: A Python class path string (e.g., 'vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler.Scheduler') or a class reference
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter controls which scheduler class vLLM uses to decide the order and batching of requests. The scheduler directly governs token-level scheduling decisions (prefill/decode batching, chunked prefill behavior, KV cache allocation), making it a primary determinant of throughput and latency.
On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend silently overrides this parameter in three scenarios (vllm_ascend/platform.py:600-612): 1. When `recompute_scheduler_enable` is set, it forces
   `vllm_ascend.core.recompute_scheduler.RecomputeScheduler` (or
   `AsyncRecomputeScheduler` if async_scheduling is enabled).
2. When `SLO_limits_for_dynamic_batch != -1`, it forces
   `vllm_ascend.core.scheduler_dynamic_batch.SchedulerDynamicBatch` and
   also enables chunked prefill.
3. When `profiling_chunk_config.enabled` is true, it forces
   `vllm_ascend.core.scheduler_profiling_chunk.ProfilingChunkScheduler`.

These Ascend-specific schedulers implement NPU-optimized batching strategies (dynamic batch sizing, recompute-aware scheduling, profiling-based chunk sizing) that can significantly outperform the upstream Scheduler on Ascend hardware. The upstream default (`vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler.Scheduler`) is GPU-optimized and may not account for Ascend's memory hierarchy and compute characteristics.
The scheduler is instantiated in `vllm/v1/engine/core.py:132` via `get_scheduler_cls()`, which resolves the class from the string path. If `scheduler_cls` is None, it selects `AsyncScheduler` when async_scheduling is enabled, otherwise the default `Scheduler`.

legacy_profiles.name: --scheduler-reserve-full-isl
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled (default), the scheduler checks whether the FULL input sequence length (ISL) of a new request fits in the KV cache before admitting it, rather than only checking the first chunk. This prevents over-admission: without this check, the scheduler might admit a request whose first chunk fits, only to later discover the full sequence cannot be accommodated, causing preemption and KV cache thrashing. The parameter is passed as `full_sequence_must_fit` to `kv_cache_manager.allocate_slots()` in both the upstream v1 scheduler (vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:711) and the vllm-ascend profiling scheduler (vllm_ascend/core/scheduler_profiling_chunk.py:587). On Ascend NPU, where KV cache memory is managed via CANN and may have different allocation granularity than GPU, preventing over-admission is critical to avoid expensive preemption cycles that involve HCCL communication for KV block swaps. Setting this to false can increase throughput by admitting more requests concurrently, but risks KV cache thrashing under high load with long sequences.

legacy_profiles.name: --scheduling-policy
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the order in which the vLLM scheduler selects requests from the waiting queue for execution. With "fcfs" (First Come First Served), requests are processed strictly in arrival order. With "priority", requests with lower priority values are scheduled earlier, with arrival time breaking ties. The performance impact is low because it only affects request ordering, not the core scheduling algorithm (e.g., token budget allocation, prefill/decode batching, or KV cache management). On Ascend NPU, the scheduling logic is identical to upstream vLLM — vllm-ascend does not override or modify this parameter. The impact is most noticeable under high load with mixed-priority workloads, where "priority" mode can reduce latency for high-priority requests at the cost of increased latency for low-priority ones. Overall system throughput remains largely unchanged.

legacy_profiles.name: shutdown-timeout
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the grace period (in seconds) during engine shutdown for in-flight requests to complete. When set to 0 (default), all running requests are immediately aborted. When set to a positive value, the engine waits up to that many seconds for requests to finish before aborting the remainder. The performance impact is low because it only affects the shutdown phase, not steady-state throughput or latency. However, in production deployments with long-running requests, a non-zero timeout can prevent unnecessary request failures during graceful rolling restarts, indirectly improving perceived latency for end users. On Ascend NPU, the behavior is identical to upstream vLLM — vllm-ascend does not override or modify this parameter. The shutdown logic in vllm/v1/engine/core.py:1240 reads `self.vllm_config.shutdown_timeout` and either aborts immediately (timeout=0) or drains requests with a deadline. The API server launcher (vllm/entrypoints/launcher.py:110) and CLI serve entrypoint (vllm/entrypoints/cli/serve.py:225,309) also use this value when propagating shutdown signals to engine processes.

legacy_profiles.name: --skip-mm-profiling
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When --skip-mm-profiling is enabled (set to true), the vLLM engine skips the memory profiling step for the multimodal encoder and encoder cache during engine initialization. In the v1 worker's profile_run method (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:5892), the code checks mm_config.skip_mm_profiling: if true, it logs a message and bypasses the encoder profiling entirely. This reduces engine startup time (lower cold-start latency) but shifts the responsibility to the user for estimating the peak memory usage of multimodal encoder activations and embedding caches. On Ascend NPU, where memory management is critical due to limited HBM capacity, skipping profiling can lead to OOM errors at runtime if the user underestimates memory requirements, or wasted memory if they overestimate. The parameter does not affect steady-state throughput directly, but incorrect memory estimation can cause request failures or suboptimal KV cache allocation, indirectly impacting throughput.

legacy_profiles.name: --stream-interval
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls how many tokens are buffered before being sent to the client during streaming. The parameter is consumed by OutputProcessor (v1 engine) and stored as `stream_interval` in RequestState. During output processing, tokens are accumulated and only flushed to the client when the accumulated count reaches `stream_interval`. A value of 1 sends each token immediately (lowest perceived latency but higher host CPU overhead per token). Larger values batch multiple tokens before sending, reducing the number of IPC/network round-trips between the engine process and the API server, which can improve throughput under high load by amortizing per-message overhead. This is purely a host-side batching optimization — it does not affect NPU computation, scheduling, or memory usage. On Ascend NPU, the effect is identical to upstream GPU behavior since it operates entirely in the output processing layer (Python-level), not in the model execution path.

legacy_profiles.name: --tensor-parallel-size
legacy_profiles.valid_choices: positive integer, typically a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8)
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
Tensor parallel size controls how many NPU devices split the model's weight matrices and compute across attention heads and hidden dimensions. On Ascend NPU, this parameter directly determines:
1. **Memory distribution**: Each NPU holds 1/tp_size of the model weights, reducing
   per-device memory pressure. This is critical for large models that exceed single-NPU
   HBM capacity.

2. **Communication overhead**: Higher tp_size introduces HCCL all-reduce/all-gather
   operations after each attention and MLP block. On Ascend, vllm-ascend may use
   FLASHCOMM1 or FLASHCOMM2 to fuse these communications with computation, but the
   overhead still grows with tp_size.

3. **Sequence parallelism interaction**: When `enable_sp` is active (FLASHCOMM1),
   vllm-ascend pads tokens to multiples of tp_size (see `_pad_for_sequence_parallelism`
   in model_runner_v1.py:2626) and adjusts cudagraph capture sizes to be multiples of
   tp_size (platform.py:459-476). This can cause token padding waste if tp_size is
   large relative to batch size.

4. **CUDAGraph capture**: The cudagraph capture sizes are validated against tp_size
   when sequence parallelism is enabled (platform.py:465-468). Mismatched sizes cause
   assertion errors.

5. **Fine-grained TP**: vllm-ascend supports per-component TP sizes via
   `finegrained_tp_config` (lmhead_tensor_parallel_size, oproj_tensor_parallel_size,
   embedding_tensor_parallel_size, mlp_tensor_parallel_size), allowing heterogeneous
   parallelism within a single model.

6. **Shared expert DP**: The `enable_shared_expert_dp` feature only activates when
   tp_size > 1 (ascend_config.py:109).

7. **World size constraint**: The product of tp_size × pp_size × pcp_size must equal
   the total world size (patch_multiproc_executor.py:33-38).

legacy_profiles.name: --video-pruning-rate
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls Efficient Video Sampling (EVS), which prunes a fraction of media tokens from each video before they enter the vision encoder and language model. The pruning rate q ∈ [0, 1) determines what fraction of tokens is dropped. For example, q=0.5 means 50% of video tokens are pruned. The pruning is applied in the multimodal processor (e.g., NanoNemotronVLProcessingInfo at vllm/model_executor/models/nano_nemotron_vl.py:524-539) via compute_retained_tokens_count(), which reduces the number of visual tokens per video frame. Since video models can produce thousands of tokens per video (num_frames × tokens_per_frame), pruning directly reduces: (1) Vision encoder compute — fewer patches to encode. (2) Language model prefill compute — fewer visual tokens to attend to. (3) KV cache memory — fewer visual token KV entries to store. (4) Decode latency — shorter sequence lengths for cross-attention or full-attention over visual tokens. On Ascend NPU, reducing token count alleviates both compute and memory pressure, which is especially beneficial given the NPU's fixed on-chip memory and the overhead of dynamic shape handling in CANN. The parameter is only effective when video_pruning_rate is not None and > 0 (checked at vllm/config/multimodal.py:338). No vllm-ascend override was found; the parameter passes through to the model's multimodal processor unchanged.

legacy_profiles.name: --worker-cls
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter determines which Worker class is instantiated to execute model inference on each device. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend silently overrides the "auto" default to select an NPU-optimized worker (NPUWorker, NPUWorker310, or XliteWorker) instead of the upstream GPU Worker. The worker class controls the entire model execution path: how attention is computed, how KV cache is managed, how communication collectives are invoked, and which Ascend-specific optimizations (e.g., custom ops, NPU graph capture) are active. Choosing the wrong worker class will either crash (if the class is incompatible with Ascend hardware) or silently fall back to suboptimal code paths, severely degrading throughput and latency. The vllm-ascend platform module (vllm_ascend/platform.py:556-566) overrides worker_cls when set to "auto" based on device type (310P vs other Ascend) and whether Xlite is enabled.

legacy_profiles.name: ASCEND_ENABLE_USE_FABRIC_MEM
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
When ASCEND_ENABLE_USE_FABRIC_MEM=1, the MooncakeBackend enables a unified memory address direct transmission scheme for KV cache transfer on Ascend 800 I/T A3 series hardware. This changes the store setup path significantly: - "Without fabric memory (default): a transfer engine is obtained via global_te.get_transfer_engine(),"
  local_seg includes the RPC port, local_buffer_size is passed to store.setup(), and the engine
  is explicitly provided. Buffers must be registered via global_te.register_buffer().
- With fabric memory: "local_seg is just the hostname (no port), local_buffer_size is forced to 0,"
  no transfer engine is obtained, and register_buffer() becomes a no-op.
The fabric memory path eliminates the need for explicit buffer registration and reduces communication overhead by using direct memory addressing, which directly improves KV cache transfer latency and throughput in Mooncake-based disaggregated prefill/decode deployments. Additionally, when fabric memory is enabled, lazy_init is also enabled (line 70), deferring store initialization until the first put() call, which can reduce startup time.

legacy_profiles.name: ASCEND_TRANSFER_TIMEOUT
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: ASCEND_TRANSFER_TIMEOUT controls the timeout for KV cache transfer operations over RDMA in Mooncake-based disaggregated prefill-decode scenarios on Ascend NPU. It is set as an environment variable and read by get_transfer_timeout_value() in vllm_ascend/distributed/kv_transfer/utils/utils.py. When not explicitly set, the default is computed as: "(4.096 * (2^HCCL_RDMA_TIMEOUT)) * HCCL_RDMA_RETRY_CNT // 1000 + 3000" milliseconds. With default HCCL_RDMA_TIMEOUT=20 and HCCL_RDMA_RETRY_CNT=7, this yields approximately 30000ms (30 seconds). The value is injected into os.environ at the start of every MooncakeConnectorWorker, MooncakeHybridConnectorWorker, and MooncakeLayerwiseConnectorWorker initialization. An insufficient timeout can cause KV transfer operations to fail prematurely under high network load or large model sizes, leading to request failures and reduced throughput. An excessively large timeout delays error detection, increasing tail latency for failed transfers. The documentation specifies that default_kv_lease_ttl must be larger than ASCEND_TRANSFER_TIMEOUT, and that ASCEND_TRANSFER_TIMEOUT must satisfy: "ASCEND_TRANSFER_TIMEOUT > RDMA_TIMEOUT * 7," where RDMA_TIMEOUT = 4.096μs * 2^HCCL_RDMA_TIMEOUT.

legacy_profiles.name: COMPILE_CUSTOM_KERNELS
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: COMPILE_CUSTOM_KERNELS controls whether vllm-ascend's custom AscendC kernels (rotary embedding, MatmulAllReduce fusion, FlashComm, and other ops) are compiled and loaded at build time and runtime. When set to False, setup.py skips the entire CMake build process (setup.py:366-367) and the build_aclnn command (setup.py:437-439), meaning no custom .so files are produced. At runtime, NPUWorker.__init__ (worker.py:93-97) checks this flag and emits a warning that "without custom kernels, vllm-ascend will not function correctly." The custom kernels provide optimized implementations of attention, rotary embedding, and communication ops that are critical for inference performance on Ascend NPUs. Without them, vllm-ascend falls back to generic PyTorch ops which are significantly slower on Da Vinci architecture. As of recent releases (v0.12.0+), this env var has been removed entirely — custom kernels are now mandatory and cannot be disabled (release_notes.md:990: "we removed the env COMPILE_CUSTOM_KERNELS. You can not set it to 0 now.").

legacy_profiles.name: DS_ENABLE_EXCLUSIVE_CONNECTION
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This environment variable controls whether the Yuanrong Datasystem client uses exclusive connection mode when communicating with the remote KV cache store. When enabled (set to "1"), it is passed to `HeteroClient.enable_exclusive_connection`, which may reduce connection contention in multi-process or multi-node deployments by dedicating a connection per client. The performance impact is indirect: "it affects the efficiency of KV cache transfer operations" (send/recv) between nodes during disaggregated prefill-decode scenarios. If connection multiplexing causes head-of-line blocking or contention, enabling exclusive connections can improve KV transfer latency and thus end-to-end throughput. However, this only applies when the Yuanrong backend is actively used for KV cache transfer; in standard vLLM deployments without disaggregated KV cache, this parameter has no effect.
