constraints: This env var only takes effect when distributed_executor_backend is set to "ray".
The value must be "0" or "1" (interpreted as boolean).

tuning_advice.summary: On Ascend NPU, test both executor backends to determine which provides better throughput and latency for your specific model and parallelism configuration. The compiled-graph backend (VLLM_USE_RAY_V2_EXECUTOR_BACKEND=0) may offer lower overhead for static computation graphs, while the V2 MQ-based backend (VLLM_USE_RAY_V2_EXECUTOR_BACKEND=1) may be more flexible and stable.

suggested_values.scenario: Default deployment on Ascend NPU with tensor parallelism, seeking stability and broad compatibility.
suggested_values.reason: The V2 MQ-based executor is the default and more widely tested path. It avoids potential compatibility issues with Ray's compiled-graph backend on Ascend HCCL.

suggested_values.scenario: Performance-sensitive deployment where the model graph is static and you want to minimize scheduling overhead.
suggested_values.reason: The compiled-graph backend pre-compiles the communication graph, which can reduce per-step scheduling overhead and improve latency for static workloads. Test with HCCL to verify stability on Ascend.

caveats:
The compiled-graph backend (VLLM_USE_RAY_V2_EXECUTOR_BACKEND=0) is more sensitive to dynamic control flow and may have stricter requirements on graph structure.
On Ascend NPU, HCCL communication behavior may differ from NCCL. The compiled-graph backend's NCCL channel type may not directly map to HCCL — test thoroughly.
The V2 MQ-based backend may have higher per-step overhead but is generally more robust for dynamic workloads and speculative decoding.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Start with the default V2 backend (1). If latency is critical and your workload is static, benchmark with the compiled-graph backend (0) to compare.

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_USE_RAY_WRAPPED_PP_COMM
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This environment variable controls which communication backend is used for pipeline-parallel (PP) tensor transfers between Ray workers when using the Ray Compiled Graph executor (v1 upstream path). When set to true (default), vLLM registers a custom RayPPCommunicator that wraps vLLM's internal _PP GroupCoordinator, using it to handle PP communication within Ray's compiled DAG. When set to false, Ray's native NCCL communicator is used instead. The choice affects the low-level transport mechanism for intermediate activations between pipeline stages. On Ascend NPU, this parameter is only relevant when using the upstream Ray executor with pipeline parallelism — vllm-ascend does not override or modify this parameter, and its own Ascend-specific executor paths do not reference it. The performance difference between the two communicator backends is typically small and workload-dependent, making this a low-impact tuning knob.

usage_locations.context: In the v1 Ray executor's _compiled_ray_dag method, this env var is checked to decide whether to register RayPPCommunicator (wrapping vLLM's PP group coordinator) or fall back to Ray's native NCCL communicator for inter-stage tensor transport.

related_parameters.name: VLLM_USE_RAY_COMPILED_DAG_CHANNEL_TYPE
related_parameters.relation: Controls the transport channel type (auto/nccl/shm) for Ray Compiled Graph PP communication; used alongside VLLM_USE_RAY_WRAPPED_PP_COMM to determine the full communication stack.

related_parameters.name: VLLM_USE_RAY_COMPILED_DAG_OVERLAP_COMM
related_parameters.relation: Enables communication overlap in Ray Compiled Graph; interacts with the PP communication backend chosen by VLLM_USE_RAY_WRAPPED_PP_COMM.

related_parameters.name: VLLM_USE_RAY_V2_EXECUTOR_BACKEND
related_parameters.relation: When true, uses RayExecutorV2 (MQ-based) instead of the compiled-graph backend, making VLLM_USE_RAY_WRAPPED_PP_COMM irrelevant since the compiled DAG path is not used.

constraints: This parameter only takes effect when using the Ray compiled-graph executor (v1 upstream path) with pipeline parallelism enabled.
Setting VLLM_USE_RAY_V2_EXECUTOR_BACKEND to true bypasses the compiled-graph path entirely, making this parameter have no effect.

tuning_advice.summary: Keep the default value (true) unless you encounter PP communication issues with Ray Compiled Graph on Ascend NPU.

suggested_values.scenario: Default usage with Ray compiled-graph executor and pipeline parallelism
suggested_values.reason: Uses vLLM's custom RayPPCommunicator which wraps the internal PP group coordinator, providing better integration with vLLM's pipeline parallelism logic.

suggested_values.scenario: Debugging PP communication issues or testing Ray native NCCL performance
suggested_values.reason: Falls back to Ray's native NCCL communicator, which may help isolate whether communication issues are related to the custom wrapper.

caveats: This parameter only affects the v1 upstream Ray executor path; vllm-ascend's own executor implementations do not use it.
On Ascend NPU, HCCL (not NCCL) is the underlying communication library, so Ray's "NCCL communicator" path may behave differently than on CUDA GPUs.
The performance difference between the two options is typically negligible for most workloads.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Leave at default (true) unless debugging PP communication problems on Ascend NPU.

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_USE_SIMPLE_KV_OFFLOAD
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This environment variable selects the KV cache offloading connector when `kv_offloading_backend` is set to "native" and `kv_offloading_size` is configured. When enabled (set to 1), it uses the "SimpleCPUOffloadConnector" instead of the default "OffloadingConnector". The connector choice directly affects how KV cache blocks are transferred between GPU/NPU memory and CPU memory during offloading, impacting memory pressure, transfer latency, and overall throughput. On Ascend NPU, KV offloading can help mitigate the typically smaller HBM capacity compared to high-end GPUs, but the simpler connector may have different performance characteristics (potentially lower overhead but less sophisticated scheduling). The parameter is read in `VllmConfig._update_kv_transfer_config` (vllm/config/vllm.py:697) during configuration initialization. No vllm-ascend override was found for this parameter, so the upstream behavior applies directly on Ascend.

usage_locations.context: Selects between "SimpleCPUOffloadConnector" and "OffloadingConnector" when kv_offloading_backend is "native" and kv_offloading_size is set.

related_parameters.name: kv_offloading_size
related_parameters.relation: Must be set (non-None) for VLLM_USE_SIMPLE_KV_OFFLOAD to have any effect. This parameter in CacheConfig triggers KV offloading activation.

related_parameters.name: kv_offloading_backend
related_parameters.relation: Must be set to "native" for VLLM_USE_SIMPLE_KV_OFFLOAD to take effect. Other backends (e.g., "lmcache") use their own connectors.

related_parameters.name: kv_transfer_config
related_parameters.relation: The KVTransferConfig object that receives the connector selection based on this env var. Its kv_connector field is set to either "SimpleCPUOffloadConnector" or "OffloadingConnector".

constraints: kv_offloading_size must be set in CacheConfig for this env var to have any effect.
kv_offloading_backend must be set to "native" for this env var to take effect.

tuning_advice.summary: Enable simple KV offload on Ascend NPU when CPU offloading is needed and you want a lightweight connector with potentially lower CPU-side overhead.

suggested_values.scenario: Ascend NPU with limited HBM, using native KV offloading to CPU, and prioritizing simplicity over advanced scheduling.
suggested_values.reason: Uses SimpleCPUOffloadConnector which may have lower CPU overhead and simpler logic, beneficial when the advanced features of OffloadingConnector are not needed.

suggested_values.scenario: Ascend NPU with native KV offloading where advanced scheduling (e.g., prefetching, eviction policies) is desired.
suggested_values.reason: Uses the default OffloadingConnector which provides more sophisticated KV block management, potentially better for complex workloads.

caveats:
This parameter only takes effect when both kv_offloading_size is set and kv_offloading_backend is "native". It is silently ignored otherwise.
On Ascend NPU, KV offloading to CPU adds PCIe/NUMA transfer latency. The simple connector may not optimize transfer scheduling as aggressively as the default connector, potentially impacting throughput under high load.
No vllm-ascend specific override exists for this parameter. The upstream behavior applies directly, but Ascend NPU memory characteristics (typically smaller HBM) make KV offloading more critical than on GPUs.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Set VLLM_USE_SIMPLE_KV_OFFLOAD=1 for lightweight CPU offloading on Ascend when using native backend; leave at 0 for advanced scheduling features.

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_USE_STANDALONE_COMPILE
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This environment variable controls whether vLLM uses PyTorch Inductor's standalone compile mode (InductorStandaloneAdaptor) instead of the default InductorAdaptor. When enabled (default), compilation is performed via torch._inductor.standalone_compile, which provides better compilation caching and reuse. The primary performance impact is on cold-start latency: standalone compile mode can significantly reduce model loading and first-inference time by enabling more efficient compilation caching. On Ascend NPU, this is particularly important because CANN graph compilation is already expensive — reducing redundant Inductor recompilation helps minimize total startup overhead. The flag is enabled by default in torch >= 2.9 and is required for VLLM_USE_MEGA_AOT_ARTIFACT to function. Disabling it falls back to the older InductorAdaptor path, which may cause longer cold-start times and less effective compilation caching.

tuning_advice.quick_guide: Keep VLLM_USE_STANDALONE_COMPILE=1 (default) on Ascend NPU to minimize cold-start compilation overhead; only set to 0 for debugging Inductor issues

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This environment variable toggles between vLLM's v1 and v2 model runner architectures. On Ascend NPU, the choice has profound performance implications because vllm-ascend maintains completely separate code paths for v1 and v2, with different attention backends, forward context handling, and feature support.
In v1 mode (VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0, default): - "vllm-ascend uses its own Ascend-native attention backends (ASCEND_DSA, ASCEND_MLA,"
  ASCEND_SFA, CUSTOM) with full feature support including context parallelism.
- "The forward context uses Ascend-specific extra attributes (is_first_layer,"
  prefetch_mlp_gate_up_proj, prefetch_mlp_gate_down_proj, prefetch_mlp_enabled,
  model_instance, is_draft_model) for optimized execution.
- "Speculative decoding supports ngram, MTP, Medusa, and Eagle through Ascend-native"
  proposers in the v1 dispatch path.

In v2 mode (VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1): - "All attention backends report as \"FLASH_ATTN\" to satisfy v2's KV cache initialization"
  assertions, potentially losing Ascend-specific optimizations.
- "The forward context uses a simplified additional_kwargs dict, lacking v1's extra"
  fields (is_first_layer, prefetch_mlp_*, model_instance, is_draft_model).
- "The platform.py MoE communication setup is only active in v2 mode, enabling"
  Ascend-specific MoE optimizations (moe_comm_method selection, in_profile_run detection).
- v2 has stricter feature validation: "it rejects routed experts capture, custom logits"
  processors, KV sharing fast prefill, and EC transfer configurations.
- "On vllm 0.21.0, v2 is explicitly unsupported and falls back to v1 with a warning." - "Hybrid models (e.g., Qwen3.5 with Mamba-style GDN + attention layers) are not"
  supported in v2 mode.

The v2 runner generally offers better scheduling and throughput on GPUs, but on Ascend NPU the v1 path has more mature Ascend-specific optimizations. The choice directly affects which attention kernels execute, how MoE communication is handled, and which speculative decoding methods are available.

tuning_advice.summary: On Ascend NPU, keep VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 (v1) for production unless you specifically need v2's MoE communication optimizations and can accept reduced attention backend support.

suggested_values.scenario: Production deployment on Ascend NPU with standard dense or MoE models
suggested_values.reason: v1 mode uses Ascend-native attention backends (ASCEND_DSA, ASCEND_MLA, ASCEND_SFA) with full feature support including context parallelism and speculative decoding (ngram, MTP, Medusa, Eagle). This is the most mature and tested path on Ascend hardware.

suggested_values.scenario: MoE model deployment where Ascend-specific MoE communication optimizations are critical
suggested_values.reason: v2 mode enables the Ascend MoE forward context setup in platform.py, which selects optimal moe_comm_method and detects profile runs. This can improve MoE throughput but sacrifices Ascend-native attention backend names and some forward context features.

suggested_values.scenario: Development or testing on vllm 0.21.0
suggested_values.reason: v2 is explicitly unsupported on vllm 0.21.0; the worker automatically falls back to v1 regardless of the env var setting.

caveats: In v2 mode, all Ascend attention backends report as "FLASH_ATTN" to pass v2's KV cache initialization assertions, which may bypass Ascend-specific attention optimizations available in v1.
v2 mode lacks v1's extra forward context fields (is_first_layer, prefetch_mlp_*, model_instance, is_draft_model), which may affect performance of pipeline-parallel or speculative decoding setups.
v2 mode has stricter feature validation and will raise errors for unsupported configurations (routed experts capture, custom logits processors, KV sharing fast prefill, EC transfer).
Hybrid models like Qwen3.5 are not supported in v2 mode.
The v2 path on Ascend is less mature; e2e tests for v2 are marked with skipif and noted as broken after CANN/triton-ascend upgrades.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Use VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 (v1) on Ascend NPU for production stability and full feature support; only enable v2 if you specifically need its MoE communication optimizations and have verified compatibility with your model.

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_V1_OUTPUT_PROC_CHUNK_SIZE
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls the maximum number of requests processed per asyncio task iteration in the V1 AsyncLLM output handler. When the engine core produces outputs, they are split into chunks of at most this size before being dispatched to individual AsyncStream objects. A larger chunk size reduces per-iteration overhead and can improve throughput, but increases the time spent in a single asyncio task, which can cause higher variance in inter-message latencies for streaming responses. A smaller chunk size yields more consistent per-token delivery latency at the cost of increased scheduling overhead and potentially lower overall throughput. This parameter only affects the V1 engine path and is read in vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:654 during output handler setup.

usage_locations.context: Read to determine chunk size for splitting engine core outputs before processing per-stream
Used in the for-loop that slices engine_core_outputs into chunks for iterative processing

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_V1_USE_OUTLINES_CACHE
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled, this env var activates an unbounded on-disk cache for compiled outlines (structured output grammars) in the vLLM V1 engine. The cache avoids recompiling the same grammar on repeated requests, which reduces per-request CPU overhead and can improve latency for workloads with a small set of recurring JSON schemas or regex constraints. On Ascend NPU, the benefit is identical to upstream: "it saves CPU-side compilation time but does not affect" NPU kernel execution. The cache is disk-backed (via diskcache) with no eviction policy, so it grows without bound. The default is false (cache disabled), in which case an in-memory LRU cache of size 128 is used instead.

usage_locations.context: Checks VLLM_V1_USE_OUTLINES_CACHE to decide whether to create an unbounded diskcache.Cache or fall back to an in-memory LRUCache(maxsize=128) for compiled outlines.

constraints: The on-disk cache is unbounded and has no eviction policy; it will grow indefinitely and may consume all available disk space if not manually cleaned.
The cache is not safe for multi-tenant environments with potentially malicious users, as noted in the source code comments.

tuning_advice.summary: Enable only if you have a stable set of structured output schemas and sufficient disk space; otherwise leave disabled to use the default in-memory LRU cache.

suggested_values.scenario: Production serving with a fixed set of JSON schemas and ample disk space
suggested_values.reason: Avoids repeated grammar compilation on every request, reducing CPU overhead and tail latency for structured output workloads.

suggested_values.scenario: General-purpose or multi-tenant deployments
suggested_values.reason: The default in-memory LRU cache (size 128) is safe, bounded, and sufficient for most workloads without risking disk exhaustion.

caveats: The on-disk cache has no size limit and no eviction; monitor disk usage and periodically clean the cache directory if enabled.
The cache is invalidated when the outlines_core package version changes, which may cause a one-time cache clear on upgrade.
This parameter only affects CPU-side grammar compilation time; it does not change NPU kernel performance or memory usage on Ascend hardware.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Enable (set to "1") only for production deployments with a fixed set of structured output schemas and sufficient disk space; keep disabled otherwise.

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_VIDEO_FETCH_TIMEOUT
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This environment variable controls the timeout (in seconds) for fetching video data from URLs when serving multimodal models. It is passed as `fetch_timeout` to the `load_from_url` / `load_from_url_async` methods in `vllm/multimodal/media/connector.py`. A higher value allows more time for slow network connections or large video downloads to complete before the request fails. A lower value causes faster failure on unreachable URLs, which can reduce tail latency for requests with invalid video URLs. This parameter does NOT affect NPU computation, memory allocation, or throughput for successful requests — it only affects the failure mode for video URL fetching. There is no vllm-ascend override; the behavior is identical on Ascend NPU.

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_WEIGHT_OFFLOADING_DISABLE_PIN_MEMORY
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This env var controls whether PyTorch's pin_memory() is used when offloading model weights back to CPU after GPU computation. When enabled (set to 1/true), it disables pin_memory for CPU-offloaded tensors. On unified-memory systems (e.g., NVIDIA GH200), pinned memory consumes GPU memory, so disabling it saves GPU memory. On Ascend NPU, the effect depends on whether the Ascend platform's is_pin_memory_available() returns true and whether CPU offloading (--cpu-offload-gb) is active. The parameter is checked in two code paths: (1) vllm/model_executor/model_loader/utils.py:155 — during the finally block of device_loading_context, when restoring parameters to CPU after temporary GPU placement; (2) vllm/model_executor/offloader/base.py:28 — in the should_pin_memory() helper used by the offloader subsystem. If CPU offloading is not active, this parameter has no effect. legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_WEIGHT_OFFLOADING_DISABLE_UVA
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This environment variable controls whether Unified Virtual Addressing (UVA) is used for CPU weight offloading. When set to 0 (default), UVA is enabled, allowing the GPU/NPU to directly access CPU-pinned memory via the system's unified virtual address space. This enables CUDA graphs (or NPU graphs) to be used alongside CPU offloading, which significantly improves throughput and reduces launch overhead. When set to 1, UVA is disabled, and the offloader falls back to a functional_call-based approach that moves parameters on-demand. This fallback path is incompatible with CUDA/NPU graphs, forcing eager execution mode (--enforce-eager), which degrades throughput and increases latency. On Ascend NPU, the same mechanism applies: disabling UVA prevents graph capture and forces eager execution, directly impacting performance. The parameter is read in vllm/model_executor/offloader/uva.py:48 to determine the offloading strategy.

legacy_profiles.name: VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This environment variable controls the Python multiprocessing start method used to create worker processes in vLLM. The choice between "fork" and "spawn" has significant implications for Ascend NPU runtime performance and stability.
On Ascend NPU, the vllm-ascend examples consistently set this to "spawn" (see examples/offline_inference_npu.py:24, examples/offline_data_parallel.py:68, examples/offline_disaggregated_prefill_npu.py:25, and others). This is because the "fork" method can cause issues with NPU device contexts and CANN runtime initialization. When using "fork", the child process inherits the parent's memory space including NPU device state, which can lead to hangs, crashes, or incorrect behavior with HCCL communication and CANN driver interactions.
The upstream vLLM CLI entrypoint (vllm/entrypoints/utils.py:169) automatically sets this to "spawn" if not already set, citing compatibility issues with accelerators. The CPU platform (vllm/platforms/cpu.py:199) and XPU platform (vllm/platforms/xpu.py:252) both force "spawn" as the only supported method.
Performance impact: "\"spawn\" creates a fresh Python interpreter for each worker," which incurs additional startup overhead (model reloading, CANN context initialization per worker). However, this is necessary for correct operation on Ascend NPU. Using "fork" may appear to start faster but can cause intermittent failures, deadlocks in HCCL collective operations, or silent correctness issues that manifest as degraded throughput or hangs under load.
The vllm-ascend documentation for large-scale expert parallelism (user_guide/feature_guide/large_scale_ep.md:206) explicitly sets this to "fork" for distributed DP server scenarios, suggesting that "fork" may be acceptable in specific multi-node configurations where workers are launched via external process managers rather than Python's multiprocessing module.
Additionally, NUMA binding (vllm/utils/numa_utils.py:297) requires "spawn" and will be silently ineffective with "fork", which can impact memory access locality and throughput on multi-socket Ascend servers.
The Whisper model architecture (vllm/config/vllm.py:1168) and torch_shm IPC for multimodal tensors (vllm/config/vllm.py:920) both require "spawn" and will raise errors or warnings if "fork" is used.

Checks for "forkserver" method for pre-import optimization

legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls the in-memory cache size for the xgrammar grammar compiler, which is used for structured output generation (JSON schema, regex, etc.). The value is converted to bytes (multiplied by 1024*1024) and passed as `cache_limit_bytes` to the xgrammar GrammarCompiler constructor in vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py:68. A larger cache allows more compiled grammars to be retained, avoiding recompilation overhead for repeated schema requests. The default 512 MB is stated to accommodate roughly 1000 JSON schemas. On Ascend NPU, this parameter affects host memory usage (not device HBM), and its performance impact is limited to structured output workloads where grammar compilation latency matters. For most deployments, the default is sufficient.

legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When using FP8 KV cache with the FlashInfer backend, this parameter controls whether the query tensor (Q) is also quantized to FP8 before the attention computation. By default (false), Q is quantized to FP8 when KV cache is FP8 and TRTLLM attention is supported, which enables the use of faster FP8 TRTLLM attention kernels. Setting this to true forces Q to remain in the model's native dtype (e.g., BF16), which may cause a fallback to slower attention kernels. This affects both prefill and decode attention paths. No vllm-ascend override or usage was found, meaning this parameter has no effect on standard Ascend deployments. legacy_profiles.name: attention.use_non_causal
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls whether the attention mechanism uses non-causal (bidirectional) masking instead of standard causal (autoregressive) masking. When set to true, each token can attend to all other tokens in the sequence, which is required for certain model architectures (e.g., embedding models like BERT, or prefix encoders in multimodal models). The parameter is read in vllm/v1/attention/selector.py:94 and passed into the AttentionSelectorConfig, which determines the attention backend selection. On Ascend NPU, the choice of attention backend directly affects which CANN operators are used (e.g., FlashAttention vs. standard attention), impacting both compute efficiency and memory usage. Non-causal attention typically requires storing the full attention matrix or using different tiling strategies, which can increase memory footprint and reduce throughput compared to causal attention that benefits from triangular masking optimizations. The actual performance impact depends on whether the model architecture genuinely requires non-causal attention — enabling it unnecessarily on causal models would degrade performance without benefit.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.backend
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend overrides the compilation backend selection at vllm_ascend/platform.py:498 via `cls.get_compile_backend()`, which sets `compilation_config.oot_compiler` to an Ascend-specific compiler. The `compilation_config.backend` field itself is validated in upstream vllm (vllm/config/compilation.py:980-987): when `mode == VLLM_COMPILE`, only `""`, `"eager"`, or `"inductor"` are accepted for piecewise compilation; custom backends raise ValueError. On Ascend, `is_cuda_alike` is False, so the default backend is NOT inductor. The actual compilation path is determined by `make_compiler()` in vllm/compilation/backends.py:101-121: `"inductor"` uses InductorAdaptor/InductorStandaloneAdaptor, `"eager"` uses EagerAdaptor (no graph optimization), and any other string is treated as a custom backend resolved via `current_platform.get_compile_backend()`. Since vllm-ascend patches the platform's `get_compile_backend()` to return an Ascend compiler, setting `backend` to a custom value effectively selects the Ascend-native compilation pipeline. Setting it to `"eager"` disables all graph-level compilation, falling back to eager execution which significantly increases latency and reduces throughput. Setting it to `"inductor"` is not supported on Ascend (is_cuda_alike=False) and may cause errors. The backend choice also affects custom op enablement (vllm/config/vllm.py:998-1005): inductor backend disables custom ops by default, while other backends enable all custom ops.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.compile_cache_save_format
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the on-disk format of the torch inductor compilation cache. When set to "binary", compiled artifacts are saved as a single binary file, which is multiprocess-safe and has lower filesystem overhead. When set to "unpacked", artifacts are saved as a directory structure, which is useful for debugging but NOT multiprocess-safe and may cause filesystem contention when multiple workers attempt to read/write simultaneously. The parameter is passed to InductorStandaloneAdaptor (vllm/compilation/backends.py:109), which is only used when VLLM_USE_STANDALONE_COMPILE=1 and the PyTorch version supports torch._inductor.standalone_compile. On Ascend NPU, torch inductor compilation is the primary backend, so this cache format affects cold-start latency (first-run compilation vs cache hit) and warm-start throughput. The "unpacked" format can cause race conditions in multi-GPU deployments, potentially leading to cache corruption and recompilation, which degrades throughput. The performance impact is low because it only affects compilation cache I/O, not the runtime execution of compiled models.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.compile_ranges_endpoints
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter defines the split points for Inductor compilation ranges, which control how many separate compiled graphs (CUDA Graphs on GPU, NPUGraphs on Ascend) are generated for different batch sizes. Each endpoint creates a boundary between compile ranges: [1, endpoints[0]], [endpoints[0]+1, endpoints[1]], ..., [endpoints[-1]+1, max_num_batched_tokens]. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend's `update_compile_ranges_split_points()` (ascend_config.py:379) automatically appends `ALLREDUCE_NORM_FUSE_THRESHOLD` to this list when both `enable_npugraph_ex` and `fuse_allreduce_rms` are enabled, ensuring a compile range boundary at the fusion threshold for matmul+allreduce fusion optimization. More split points mean more compiled graphs, which increases compilation time and memory but allows better specialization for each batch size range, potentially improving throughput. Fewer split points reduce compilation overhead but may result in less optimized execution for certain batch sizes. The upstream vllm code (vllm/config/vllm.py:1744-1752) validates that all endpoints are positive integers and merges them with automatically computed endpoints from fusion passes (rope+kvcache fusion, MiniMax QK norm fusion).

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.compile_sizes
legacy_profiles.valid_choices: list of positive integers, or the string 'cudagraph_capture_sizes'
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: compile_sizes controls which batch sizes are pre-compiled and warmed up during model initialization. On Ascend NPU, the vllm-ascend worker (vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py:502) reads this list and performs dummy runs for each size in descending order. These warmup runs trigger CANN graph compilation and kernel auto-tuning for those specific batch sizes. Without explicit compile_sizes, only sizes covered by cudagraph_capture_sizes or compile_ranges get compiled. For sizes not pre-compiled, the first inference request at that batch size incurs JIT compilation latency (typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds on Ascend), causing tail latency spikes. The parameter also feeds into PiecewiseBackend (vllm/compilation/piecewise_backend.py:154) which compiles separate FX graph variants for each specified size, enabling shape-specialized kernels. On Ascend, this is critical because CANN's graph compiler produces more efficient graphs when it knows the exact batch size at compile time rather than using dynamic shapes.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.cudagraph_copy_inputs
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When cudagraph_copy_inputs is True, the compilation backend copies input tensors to internally managed buffers before executing the cudagraph. This ensures that the same input buffers are always used, which is required for cudagraph correctness when callers cannot guarantee buffer reuse. The copy operation adds a small per-invocation overhead (memory allocation + copy) and increases peak memory usage due to the additional buffer allocation. On Ascend NPU, this parameter is only relevant when cudagraph_mode is not NONE (i.e., cudagraphs are enabled). vllm-ascend does not override or modify this parameter; it inherits the upstream behavior. The parameter has no effect when cudagraph_mode is NONE, as the copy logic is skipped entirely in that case.

If cudagraph_mode is NONE or cudagraph_copy_inputs is False, the function returns a VllmSerializableFunction without input copying. Otherwise, symbolic tensor indices are identified and input buffers are allocated for copying.

Checked when loading a compiled graph from cache. If True, input buffers are allocated and a copy-and-call wrapper is created around the runtime callable. If False, the runtime callable is used directly without copying.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.cudagraph_mm_encoder
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled, this parameter triggers CUDA graph capture for the multimodal encoder (e.g., ViT) in vLLM's v1 worker path. The encoder forward pass is captured as a CUDA graph for each token budget level, which can reduce kernel launch overhead and improve latency for multimodal models. However, on Ascend NPU, CUDA graphs are not natively supported — vllm-ascend replaces CUDA graph mechanisms with Ascend-specific graph capture (e.g., torch_npu graph or CANN graph). The cudagraph_mm_encoder flag is only checked in the upstream v1 GPU model runner (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:6165) and has no corresponding override or handling in vllm-ascend's v1 or v2 worker paths. As a result, this parameter has no effect on Ascend NPU runtime — the encoder CUDA graph manager is never initialized on NPU because the Ascend worker does not read this flag. The performance impact is classified as low because it is effectively a no-op on Ascend hardware.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.cudagraph_mode
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls the graph capture strategy on Ascend NPU, which directly determines whether kernel launch overhead is eliminated via ACLGraph (torch.npu.NPUGraph) capture/replay. On Ascend, the effective mode is heavily overridden by vllm-ascend in platform.py: if xlite full mode is enabled, it is forced to NONE; if xlite decode-only mode is enabled, it is forced to FULL_DECODE_ONLY; if enforce_eager is True, it is forced to NONE; if compilation mode is not NONE or VLLM_COMPILE, it is forced to NONE. In v1 worker, the mode determines whether cudagraph_batch_sizes are populated (model_runner_v1.py:533) and whether full graph streams are created. In v2 worker, has_full_cudagraphs() controls creation of an update stream for full graph parameter updates (model_runner.py:131). The mode also gates paged attention usage (attention/utils.py:51) — only FULL_DECODE_ONLY enables paged attention for supported shapes. Additionally, FULL_DECODE_ONLY is incompatible with AscendFAImpl attention backend (fa3_v1.py:54-60), which raises ValueError. Npugraph_ex (compile-time FX graph optimization) is enabled by default only for FULL and FULL_DECODE_ONLY modes, providing additional performance gains.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.cudagraph_num_of_warmups
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls how many dummy forward passes are executed before CUDA graph (or ACLGraph on Ascend) capture begins. During warmup runs, the model runs in eager mode to stabilize memory allocations and kernel launch overheads. Only after warmup is the graph captured and reused for subsequent runs. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend hardcodes this value to 1 in platform.py:442, overriding any user configuration. The warmup itself adds a small one-time overhead during engine startup (typically a few seconds), but has no effect on steady-state throughput or latency. Since the value is forced to 1 on Ascend, users cannot tune it — the performance impact is limited to the fixed startup cost.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.cudagraph_specialize_lora
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls whether separate CUDA graphs are captured for inference with and without active LoRA adapters. When true (default), two sets of graphs are captured: one for no-LoRA cases and one for LoRA-active cases. This avoids running LoRA kernel overhead when no adapters are loaded, improving throughput for mixed workloads. When false, only LoRA-enabled graphs are captured and used for all cases, meaning LoRA ops execute even when no adapters are active — incurring unnecessary compute overhead. On Ascend NPU, CUDA graphs are implemented via Ascend Graph (torch_npu graph capture), and the same specialization logic applies. Additionally, when cudagraph_specialize_lora is true and num_active_loras > 0, CUDA graphs are disabled for the speculative drafter model (see gpu_model_runner.py:5662-5665), which is a workaround for issue #28334. This means enabling specialization can cause the drafter to fall back to eager execution, potentially reducing speculative decoding throughput.

usage_locations.context: Determines whether to capture separate CUDA graphs for LoRA vs non-LoRA cases. When true, returns [0] + captured_lora_counts; when false, returns only [max_loras + 1] (LoRA-only graphs).
When true and num_active_loras > 0, disables CUDA graphs for the speculative drafter model as a workaround for a known issue.

related_parameters.relation: Both parameters affect which CUDA graph variants are captured; capture_sizes controls batch size dimensions while cudagraph_specialize_lora controls LoRA adapter dimensions.

When set to true and LoRA is active, CUDA graphs are forcibly disabled for the speculative drafter model.

suggested_values.reason: Allows the no-LoRA path to skip LoRA kernel overhead, improving throughput for non-LoRA requests. The cost is additional graph memory for the second set of graphs.

caveats: On Ascend NPU, graph capture (Ascend Graph) has higher memory overhead than CUDA GPUs; capturing two sets of graphs doubles this cost.

tuning_advice.quick_guide: Set to false if LoRA is always active or if using speculative decoding; keep true only for mixed LoRA/non-LoRA workloads without speculation.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.custom_ops
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls which custom ops (e.g., fused_moe, quant_fp8, grouped_topk, apply_rotary_emb) are dispatched at runtime. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend forcibly sets custom_ops to ["all"] for all devices except 310P (vllm_ascend/platform.py:572), overriding any user-specified value. This activates Ascend-optimized kernel implementations (forward_oot path in custom_op.py:204-205) which directly affect compute throughput, memory bandwidth utilization, and kernel launch overhead. Disabling custom ops falls back to PyTorch-native implementations, which are typically much slower on NPU hardware. The parameter also influences whether certain ops get compiled via torch.compile (custom_op.py:191-194) — when custom ops are disabled, forward_native may still be compiled, but the optimized Ascend-specific kernel is lost.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.disabled_custom_ops
legacy_profiles.valid_choices: list of custom op name strings
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter is a set (list) of custom op names that are explicitly disabled during compilation. When a custom op is in this set, vLLM falls back to the native PyTorch implementation (forward_native) instead of using the device-specific optimized kernel (forward_cuda, forward_hip, forward_oot, etc.). On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend registers its ops as out-of-tree (OOT) custom ops. If an Ascend-optimized custom op is added to disabled_custom_ops, the system will use forward_native instead of forward_oot, potentially losing NPU-specific optimizations. This directly affects compute efficiency and thus latency/throughput. The parameter is populated automatically when a CustomOp's enabled() method returns False, but can also be set via compilation config.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.dynamic_shapes_config.type
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Controls how torch.compile() handles dynamic shapes during graph capture and guard evaluation. The type affects whether guards are inserted (BACKED), omitted entirely (UNBACKED), or handled with size-oblivious semantics (BACKED_SIZE_OBLIVIOUS). On Ascend NPU, this directly impacts compilation cache hit rates and recompilation frequency. When guards fail at runtime due to shape mismatches, torch.compile triggers expensive recompilation, increasing latency and reducing throughput. UNBACKED avoids guard failures but may cause data-dependent errors. BACKED_SIZE_OBLIVIOUS is an experimental middle ground. The parameter is read in vllm/compilation/wrapper.py:103 to configure guard_filter_fn — when evaluate_guards is true and type is BACKED, shape guards are filtered to only SHAPE_ENV types, and counter-0/1 specializations are relaxed (backends.py:1234-1249). In decorators.py:522, the type is accessed during AOT compilation path setup. No vllm-ascend override was found for this parameter, so upstream behavior applies on Ascend NPU.

It is not a user-facing configuration parameter — it is populated automatically by the CustomOp.dispatch_forward() method (vllm/model_executor/custom_op.py:187) based on each op's enabled() check and _enforce_enable flag. The set is used by the compilation config to know which ops should use platform-specific (e.g., Ascend OOT) implementations vs. the native PyTorch fallback. On Ascend NPU, when current_platform.is_out_of_tree() returns True, enabled custom ops will dispatch to forward_oot() (line 204-205), which by default delegates to forward_native(). The performance impact is indirect: this set controls whether certain ops use optimized platform kernels or fallback paths, but the set itself is a passive tracker, not a tuning knob. No vllm-ascend override was found for this specific field.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.encoder_cudagraph_max_frames_per_batch
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the maximum total video frames per batch for encoder CUDA graph capture. It determines the size of the cu_seqlens buffer (one entry per attention sequence, i.e. one per video frame) used during CUDA graph capture for encoder models. On Ascend NPU, CUDA graphs are not natively supported — vllm-ascend uses its own graph capture mechanism (torch_npu graph or CANN-based compilation). The parameter may affect memory allocation for the cu_seqlens buffer and the number of encoder CUDA graph instances captured. However, since encoder CUDA graphs are primarily relevant for multimodal models with video input, and Ascend NPU has limited CUDA graph support, the practical performance impact is low for most Ascend deployments. The parameter was not found in vllm-ascend source code, suggesting it has no Ascend-specific override and follows upstream vLLM behavior where applicable.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.fast_moe_cold_start
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls whether vLLM's compilation system uses a "cold start" optimization for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers. When enabled (true), the system assumes that the only decoder forward pass being run is the current model, allowing it to pre-compute and cache the set of all MoE layers (static_all_moe_layers) rather than discovering them dynamically at runtime. This avoids a warm-up compilation step for MoE layers, reducing initial latency and compilation overhead. On Ascend NPU, where compilation (via CANN) is already a significant overhead, this can meaningfully reduce cold-start time for MoE models. However, the optimization is unsafe when speculative decoding is used with a draft model that also contains MoE layers, or when models conditionally execute different MoE branches (e.g., Ernie4.5-VL). The parameter is automatically forced to false on torch >= 2.11 (where OpaqueObject supersedes it) and for models that explicitly disable it. When left as None (default), vLLM conservatively disables it if speculative decoding is detected.

usage_locations.context: Forced to false on torch >= 2.11 (HAS_OPAQUE_TYPE); otherwise resolved from None to false if speculative_config is present, true otherwise.

Ernie4.5-VL model explicitly disables this optimization because it conditionally executes text/vision MoE branches, which would produce incorrect execution order with fast_moe_cold_start.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.inductor_compile_config
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter is a dictionary that is directly passed to torch._inductor.config to control the behavior of the PyTorch Inductor compiler backend. On Ascend NPU, vLLM uses torch.compile with the inductor backend for graph-level optimizations (e.g., kernel fusion, memory planning, autotuning). The keys in this dict correspond to inductor configuration options such as max_autotune, epilogue_fusion, size_asserts, etc. These settings affect:
1. Compilation time vs. runtime performance tradeoff (e.g., max_autotune increases
   compile time but can produce faster kernels).
2. Memory usage (e.g., enabling certain fusions may reduce intermediate tensor
   allocations).
3. Kernel launch overhead (e.g., epilogue_fusion merges pointwise operations into
   a single kernel, reducing launch overhead on NPU).

On Ascend NPU, the inductor backend generates code that is further compiled by the CANN compiler. Inductor configurations that work well on GPU may have different effects on Ascend due to differences in the Da Vinci architecture and CANN's own fusion passes. For example, excessive fusion may conflict with CANN's graph optimization, and autotuning may select suboptimal configurations for Ascend's memory hierarchy.
vLLM internally sets some defaults: "enable_auto_functionalized_v2 is forced to" False (line 895), and on PyTorch < 2.12, assertion configs (size_asserts, alignment_asserts, scalar_asserts) are tied to VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL (line 907-914). On CPU platforms, additional defaults are applied (dce, epilogue_fusion, etc. at vllm/platforms/cpu.py:170-178). No Ascend-specific overrides were found in vllm-ascend, meaning the upstream inductor config is used as-is on NPU.

usage_locations.context: Sets default inductor config values (enable_auto_functionalized_v2=False, assertion configs based on logging level)
Deep-copies inductor_compile_config into VllmBackend.inductor_config for use during compilation
Passes inductor_compile_config as options to torch.compile when backend is 'inductor'
CPU model runner reads inductor_compile_config to set freezing based on max_autotune
CPU platform applies additional inductor defaults (dce, epilogue_fusion, cpp.dynamic_threads)

tuning_advice.quick_guide: Use default empty dict on Ascend NPU; only add max_autotune or epilogue_fusion after confirming they don't cause CANN compilation errors in your model.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.mode
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: compilation.mode controls whether torch.compile-based compilation is applied to the model. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend overrides this parameter in platform.py: if enforce_eager is True, mode is forced to CompilationMode.NONE (0). If mode is set to anything other than NONE (0) or VLLM_COMPILE (3), vllm-ascend logs a warning and disables CUDAGraphs by setting cudagraph_mode to NONE. This means only modes 0 and 3 are effectively supported on Ascend. Mode 0 (NONE) runs the model in fully eager PyTorch mode with no torch.compile optimization, which increases operator dispatch overhead and reduces throughput. Mode 3 (VLLM_COMPILE) enables vLLM's custom Inductor-based compilation backend with caching, piecewise compilation, and shape specialization, which can significantly reduce latency and improve throughput. The mode also indirectly affects CUDAGraph behavior: "when mode is not NONE or VLLM_COMPILE," CUDAGraphs are disabled entirely, losing the operator dispatch reduction benefits of graph capture. Additionally, when enforce_eager is set (e.g., via xlite full mode), mode is forced to NONE, which also disables CUDAGraphs and torch.compile, resulting in the highest latency and lowest throughput configuration.

tuning_advice.quick_guide: Set compilation.mode to 3 (VLLM_COMPILE) for production; use 0 (NONE) only for debugging or when xlite full mode is required

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.pass_config.enable_qk_norm_rope_fusion
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled, this flag activates the QKNormRoPEFusionPass in the Inductor post-grad pass pipeline (vllm/compilation/passes/pass_manager.py:181-183). This pass fuses the Q/K RMSNorm and Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) operations into a single kernel, reducing the number of GPU kernel launches and intermediate memory accesses during the attention computation. Additionally, enabling this flag automatically appends "+rotary_embedding" to the custom_ops list (vllm/config/compilation.py:934-939), which forces the Inductor to treat rotary embedding as a custom operator rather than decomposing it, further enabling fusion opportunities. The net effect is reduced latency per attention layer and improved throughput, particularly for models with many attention heads or long sequences where RoPE computation is significant. However, this is a compilation-time optimization that only takes effect when compilation mode is VLLM_COMPILE (not eager execution). On Ascend NPU, the actual performance gain depends on CANN's ability to fuse these operations — the Inductor fusion pass generates a fused graph, but CANN's own graph compiler may or may not further optimize it. The flag is disabled by default.

usage_locations.context: When enable_qk_norm_rope_fusion is True, appends "+rotary_embedding" to custom_ops to prevent Inductor from decomposing RoPE, enabling the fusion pass to match the pattern.
When enable_qk_norm_rope_fusion is True, adds SplitCoalescingPass and QKNormRoPEFusionPass to the post-grad pass pipeline for fusing Q/K norm and RoPE.
Test configuration disables this fusion for sparse MLA models (e.g., DSv3.2) due to a known inductor assertion bug when +rotary_embedding is forced into the compile graph.

constraints: This flag only takes effect when compilation mode is VLLM_COMPILE; in eager execution mode the fusion pass is not applied.
Sparse MLA models (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2) may hit an inductor assertion error when this flag is enabled due to a known torch bug with +rotary_embedding in the compile graph.

tuning_advice.summary: Enable this flag for models with Q/K RMSNorm + RoPE to reduce kernel launch overhead, but verify correctness on Ascend NPU as CANN may handle fusion differently than CUDA.

suggested_values.scenario: Standard dense transformer models (e.g., Llama, Qwen) with Q/K RMSNorm and RoPE, running with VLLM_COMPILE mode on Ascend NPU.
suggested_values.reason: Fuses Q/K norm and RoPE into a single kernel, reducing GPU kernel launches and improving attention computation throughput. The automatic "+rotary_embedding" custom op prevents Inductor decomposition, enabling the fusion pattern match.

suggested_values.scenario: Sparse MLA models (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2) or models where compilation correctness is prioritized over minor latency gains.
suggested_values.reason: Sparse MLA models have a known inductor assertion bug when +rotary_embedding is forced into the compile graph. Disabling avoids compilation failures. Also appropriate when debugging or when CANN's own graph compiler already provides equivalent fusion.

caveats:
On Ascend NPU, the Inductor-generated fused kernel is ultimately compiled by CANN. CANN may apply its own fusion passes, so the net performance gain from this flag may be smaller than on CUDA. Benchmark with and without this flag on your specific Ascend hardware.
Enabling this flag automatically adds "+rotary_embedding" to custom_ops, which affects the entire compilation graph. If you have manually set custom_ops, be aware of this side effect.
This is a compilation-time optimization only. It has no effect in eager execution mode or when use_inductor_graph_partition results in piecewise compilation that does not include the attention layers.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Enable for dense models with VLLM_COMPILE on Ascend NPU to reduce attention kernel overhead; disable for sparse MLA models or when debugging compilation.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.pass_config.enable_sp
legacy_profiles.default: None (resolved to False if not explicitly set)
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: Sequence parallelism (SP) shards the sequence dimension across tensor-parallel ranks, reducing per-device activation memory and enabling larger batch sizes. On Ascend NPU, when enable_sp is True, vllm-ascend injects two graph fusion passes (SequenceParallelismPass and SequenceParallelismMoePass) that rewrite the computation graph to insert all-gather / reduce-scatter collectives at layer boundaries. This directly affects throughput and latency: "at small token counts the fixed communication" overhead dominates and hurts performance, but at larger token counts (>= sp_min_token_num, default 1000 on Ascend) the memory savings allow higher batch sizes and net throughput gains. The parameter also forces full-graph compilation (splitting_ops is cleared) and requires cudagraph capture sizes to be multiples of tensor_parallel_size, which can constrain scheduling flexibility. On Ascend, the platform layer auto-sets sp_min_token_num to 1000 for dense models and 1 for MoE models when enable_sp is True and sp_min_token_num is unset.

Updates cudagraph capture sizes to be multiples of tp_size when SP is enabled

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.pass_config.fuse_act_quant
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled, this flag activates the ActivationQuantFusionPass during the post-grad compilation phase. This pass fuses the SiLU activation + element-wise multiplication (SiluMul) with the subsequent dynamic per-token FP8 quantization operation into a single fused kernel. On Ascend NPU, this fusion eliminates intermediate tensor materialization and reduces kernel launch overhead, which directly improves the latency of the activation-quantization sequence in FP8-quantized models. The pass is applied unconditionally when fuse_act_quant=True — there is no Ascend-specific guard in the upstream code, meaning it will be attempted on Ascend hardware. However, the actual effectiveness depends on whether the torch.compile backend (e.g., torch_npu / CANN graph capture) can successfully fuse the pattern on Da Vinci architecture. If the backend cannot fuse the pattern, the pass may be a no-op or could even introduce graph breaks, negating the benefit. The parameter also affects the compilation cache UUID, so toggling it will trigger recompilation.

usage_locations.context: Checks fuse_act_quant in PostGradPassManager.configure() to conditionally add ActivationQuantFusionPass and RocmAiterSiluMulFp8GroupQuantFusionPass (ROCm only).
Test verifying that toggling fuse_act_quant changes the pass manager UUID, confirming it affects compilation cache keying.
Test for ActivationQuantFusionPass correctness, setting fuse_act_quant=True in PassConfig to enable the fusion pass during model compilation.

related_parameters.name: compilation.custom_ops

suggested_values.scenario: FP8-quantized model inference on Ascend NPU with torch.compile enabled
suggested_values.reason: Fuses the activation path (SiLU + element-wise multiply + FP8 quantization) into one kernel, reducing intermediate tensor writes and kernel launch overhead. This is particularly beneficial on Ascend NPUs where kernel launch latency can be significant.

suggested_values.scenario: Non-FP8 models or models without SiLU activation (e.g., GELU-based models)
suggested_values.reason: The fusion pattern will not match any operations in the graph, so the pass is a no-op. Keeping it disabled avoids unnecessary graph analysis overhead during compilation.

caveats: The fusion pass is upstream vLLM code with no Ascend-specific adaptation. Its effectiveness on Ascend NPU depends on whether the torch_npu/CANN backend can successfully compile the fused pattern. Test with a small benchmark before deploying in production.
Toggling this flag changes the compilation cache key (UUID), so enabling/disabling it will trigger a full recompilation of affected models.
This pass only fuses SiLU+Mul+Quant patterns. Models using other activation functions (GELU, ReLU) or static quantization schemes will not benefit.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Enable for FP8 models with SiLU activation on Ascend NPU; benchmark to confirm fusion actually occurs in the compiled graph.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.pass_config.fuse_allreduce_rms
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled, this parameter activates a compilation pass that fuses the all-reduce communication operation with the subsequent RMS normalization into a single kernel. On Ascend NPU, this is implemented via the vllm-ascend Matmul Allreduce Rmsnorm fusion Pass (PR #5034). The fusion eliminates the overhead of launching separate kernels for all-reduce and RMS norm, and reduces intermediate data movement between NPU cores and memory. This directly reduces the latency of each transformer layer that contains this pattern, improving end-to-end throughput. However, the vllm-ascend documentation explicitly notes that this pass is disabled by default because it conflicts with Sequence Parallelism (SP). When SP is enabled, enabling this fusion may cause incorrect results or compilation errors. The parameter is read in vllm/config/vllm.py:1661 to determine compile ranges for flashinfer/aiter allreduce fusion, and in vllm/compilation/passes/pass_manager.py:145 to register the appropriate fusion pass (RocmAiterAllReduceFusionPass for ROCm/aiter backends, or AllReduceFusionPass for others). On Ascend, the vllm-ascend plugin provides its own implementation of this pass.

usage_locations.context: Checks fuse_allreduce_rms to compute compile range endpoints for flashinfer/aiter allreduce fusion, adjusting max_token_num based on allreduce max size and model hidden size.
Registers the AllReduceFusionPass or RocmAiterAllReduceFusionPass when fuse_allreduce_rms is True.
Defines the Ascend-specific default (False) and documents the conflict with Sequence Parallelism.

related_parameters.relation: When fuse_allreduce_rms is enabled and ROCm aiter ops are not in use, flashinfer_max_size(tp_size) determines the maximum token count for which fusion is applied.

suggested_values.scenario: Standard deployment without Sequence Parallelism on Ascend NPU (v1-ascend or v2-ascend).
suggested_values.reason: Fuses all-reduce and RMS norm into a single kernel, reducing kernel launch overhead and intermediate data movement, which improves both latency and throughput.

suggested_values.scenario: Deployment with Sequence Parallelism enabled on Ascend NPU.
suggested_values.reason: The vllm-ascend documentation explicitly states that fuse_allreduce_rms conflicts with SP. Enabling both may cause incorrect results or compilation errors.

caveats:
On Ascend NPU, this pass is disabled by default (False) due to a known conflict with Sequence Parallelism. Always verify that SP is disabled before enabling this fusion.
The fusion pass is only effective for models that use RMS normalization followed by an all-reduce operation in tensor-parallel configurations. For models without this pattern, enabling the flag has no effect.
The maximum token count for which fusion is applied is determined by the allreduce max size (from flashinfer or aiter ops) divided by (hidden_size * dtype_size). For very large batch sizes, the fusion may not be applied to all tokens.
tuning_advice.quick_guide: Set to true on Ascend NPU when SP is disabled; keep false (default) when SP is enabled.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.pass_config.fuse_attn_quant
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled, this flag activates two torch.compile fusion passes: AttnQuantFusionPass and MLAAttnQuantFusionPass. These passes fuse the custom attention operation (or MLA attention for DeepSeek-style models) with subsequent quantization operations into a single compiled kernel. This eliminates intermediate tensor materialization and reduces kernel launch overhead, which can improve latency and throughput for quantized models (e.g., FP8). However, enabling this flag has a significant side effect: it forces cudagraph_mode to FULL (disabling piecewise cudagraphs) when use_inductor_graph_partition is off, because the fused attention+quant op is incompatible with piecewise cudagraph capture boundaries. On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend currently only supports sequence parallelism in eager mode (noted in set_splitting_ops_for_v1), so the interaction between this fusion pass and Ascend's compilation pipeline may differ from GPU behavior. The flag also ensures that attention ops are removed from splitting_ops, which affects how the FX graph is partitioned for compilation.

usage_locations.context: In set_splitting_ops_for_v1: when fuse_attn_quant is True and use_inductor_graph_partition is False, calls set_splitting_ops_for_attn_fusion() to configure graph splitting boundaries.
In set_splitting_ops_for_attn_fusion: asserts fuse_attn_quant is True, then forces cudagraph_mode to FULL if piecewise cudagraphs were configured, and ensures attention ops are not in splitting_ops.
In PostGradPassManager.__init__: when fuse_attn_quant is True, adds AttnQuantFusionPass and MLAAttnQuantFusionPass to the compilation pipeline.

related_parameters.name: compilation_config.cudagraph_mode

related_parameters.name: compilation_config.use_inductor_graph_partition
related_parameters.relation: When True, the cudagraph mode override does not occur; the fusion pass works with inductor's own graph partitioning.

related_parameters.name: compilation_config.splitting_ops
related_parameters.relation: When fuse_attn_quant is True, attention ops are removed from splitting_ops to avoid conflicts with the fused kernel.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.pass_config.fuse_rope_kvcache
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: When enabled, this parameter activates a series of compilation passes (SplitCoalescingPass, ScatterSplitReplacementPass, and RopeKVCacheFusionPass) that fuse the QK rotary position embedding (RoPE) operation with the KV cache update into a single kernel. This fusion reduces kernel launch overhead and improves data locality by eliminating intermediate memory reads/writes between the RoPE computation and the KV cache store. On Ascend NPU, kernel fusion is particularly beneficial because it reduces the number of discrete operator invocations that must be dispatched to the CANN runtime, lowering CPU-NPU synchronization overhead. The parameter also triggers the addition of "+rotary_embedding" to the custom ops list, which influences how Inductor handles the RoPE operation during compilation. However, this fusion has constraints: it requires either Inductor graph partition to be enabled or splitting_ops to be explicitly set to an empty list; otherwise the parameter is silently disabled with a warning. Additionally, the fusion can be restricted to a maximum token count via the related parameter rope_kvcache_fusion_max_token_num, which creates a compile range endpoint to limit fusion to smaller batch sizes where it is most effective.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.pass_config.sp_min_token_num
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the minimum number of tokens required for Sequence Parallelism (SP) to activate during graph compilation. SP splits the residual tensor across tensor-parallel ranks, reducing per-rank memory and communication volume for large token counts. However, when the token count is small, the fixed overhead of all-gather communication operators dominates, causing SP to degrade performance rather than improve it. The parameter acts as a threshold: "SP is only applied to graph compilation ranges where num_tokens >= sp_min_token_num." On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend overrides the default value to 1000 for dense models and 1 for MoE models (via NPUPlatform.apply_config_platform_defaults), whereas upstream vLLM computes it from hidden_size, tp_size, and element_size. Setting this too low causes SP to activate on small batches, increasing latency due to communication overhead. Setting it too high prevents SP from activating even when it would be beneficial, missing throughput gains on large batches. The value is also capped by max_num_batched_tokens to avoid exceeding scheduler limits.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.splitting_ops
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter controls which operators are excluded from CUDA graphs during piecewise compilation. On Ascend NPU, its behavior is significantly constrained by vllm-ascend overrides:
1. **Eager mode override (vllm-ascend):** When `enforce_eager=True` (which can be triggered by
   xlite full mode or model config), vllm-ascend sets `compilation_config.mode = CompilationMode.NONE`
   and forces `splitting_ops = []` if it was None (vllm_ascend/platform.py:439-440). This means
   splitting_ops has no effect in eager mode — all compilation is disabled.

2. **Piecewise CUDA graph requirement (upstream):** For piecewise CUDA graphs to work,
   `splitting_ops` must be non-empty AND `compilation_config.mode` must be `VLLM_COMPILE`
   (vllm/config/compilation.py:611). If splitting_ops is empty while cudagraph_mode is
   PIECEWISE or FULL_AND_PIECEWISE, upstream code downgrades the cudagraph mode
   (vllm/config/compilation.py:1125-1150).

3. **Full-graph compilation requirement (upstream):** Several advanced compilation passes
   (SequenceParallelismPass, AsyncTPPass) assert that splitting_ops must be empty OR
   use_inductor_graph_partition must be True — they require full-graph compilation
   (vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/sequence_parallelism.py:602-605,
   vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/collective_fusion.py:970-973,
   vllm/v1/worker/utils.py:533-536). If splitting_ops is non-empty without inductor
   graph partition, these optimizations are disabled.

4. **FX-level vs Inductor-level splitting (upstream):** When `use_inductor_graph_partition=False`
   (default), splitting_ops is used for Dynamo FX-level graph splitting
   (vllm/compilation/backends.py:1165-1171). When True, Inductor handles partitioning
   and splitting_ops is passed to inductor partition rules instead
   (vllm/compilation/backends.py:155-158).

5. **NPU compilation mode restriction (vllm-ascend):** vllm-ascend only supports
   CompilationMode.NONE and CompilationMode.VLLM_COMPILE. Any other mode triggers
   cudagraph_mode = NONE (vllm_ascend/platform.py:444-449). This limits the effective
   combinations of splitting_ops and cudagraph modes on Ascend.

Performance impact: "On Ascend NPU, splitting_ops directly affects whether piecewise CUDA graphs" can be used, which impacts decode latency and throughput. Empty splitting_ops with piecewise cudagraph modes causes silent downgrade to FULL or NONE, potentially losing performance. Non-empty splitting_ops prevents sequence parallelism and async TP optimizations from being applied, which can reduce throughput for large-batch scenarios.

legacy_profiles.name: compilation.use_inductor_graph_partition
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter controls whether Inductor-based graph partitioning is used to split the computation graph at cudagraph_unsafe operations. When enabled, graph splitting happens at Inductor codegen time after all passes and fusions are finished, rather than using Dynamo-based piecewise splitting. This affects three key areas on Ascend NPU:
1. **CUDA Graph wrapping strategy**: When use_inductor_graph_partition is true and piecewise cudagraphs are enabled, vLLM uses a custom partition wrapper (vllm/compilation/decorators.py:743) that wraps each Inductor partition with the platform's static graph wrapper class. On Ascend, this means NPU graph capture happens per-partition rather than on the full graph, which can reduce memory pressure but may increase graph capture overhead.
2. **Sequence Parallelism (SP) compatibility**: Both SequenceParallelismPass (vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/sequence_parallelism.py:603) and AsyncTPPass (vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/collective_fusion.py:971) assert that use_inductor_graph_partition must be true when splitting_ops is set, because these passes require full-graph compilation mode. On Ascend NPU with tensor parallelism, enabling SP can improve throughput for large batch sizes by distributing sequence dimensions across TP ranks.
3. **ROCm AITER rotary embedding fusion**: The enable_rope_kvcache_fusion function (vllm/config/vllm.py:152) checks use_inductor_graph_partition as a gating condition for rotary embedding custom op fusion. While this is primarily a ROCm feature, the code path exists in the shared compilation config.
On Ascend NPU, the primary performance impact comes from the interaction with piecewise CUDA graph mode and sequence parallelism. Enabling this parameter allows SP passes to function, which can significantly improve throughput for large-batch inference on multi-NPU setups, but may increase compilation time and memory fragmentation due to per-partition graph capture.

legacy_profiles.name: ec_transfer.ec_buffer_size
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the buffer size (in bytes) for the TorchDistributedConnector used in vllm-ascend's expert-parallel (EP) communication path. During MoE model inference, tokens are dispatched to and combined from different experts across EP ranks. The connector uses a fixed-size buffer to batch these token transfers. A larger buffer reduces the number of communication rounds (improving throughput) but increases peak memory usage. A smaller buffer saves memory but increases communication overhead, potentially reducing throughput. The recommended value from the code hint is 1e9 (approximately 1GB), which balances throughput and memory for typical deployments.

legacy_profiles.impact_detail: The `ec_transfer.ec_connector` parameter selects the EC (Encoder Cache) connector implementation used for transmitting encoder caches (e.g., multimodal embeddings) between vLLM instances in a disaggregated serving setup. The connector is instantiated by `ECConnectorFactory.create_connector` (vllm/distributed/ec_transfer/ec_connector/factory.py:36), which reads `ec_transfer_config.ec_connector` at line 63 to determine the connector class. The connector is used in two roles: "a scheduler-side connector that co-locates with the" scheduler process, and a worker-side connector that co-locates with worker processes. On the worker side, `ECConnectorModelRunnerMixin` (vllm/v1/worker/ec_connector_model_runner_mixin.py:14) calls `maybe_save_ec_to_connector` and `maybe_get_ec_connector_output` to save and retrieve encoder caches. The choice of connector directly affects the latency of cache transfer operations and the throughput of multimodal request processing. Different connectors may use different transport mechanisms (shared memory, NCCL, TCP, etc.) with varying performance characteristics. On Ascend NPU, the connector must be compatible with HCCL communication and CANN memory management. The vllm-ascend patch at vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py:9 imports `ECConnectorMetadata` from the base connector module, indicating that EC connector functionality is used in Ascend's balance scheduling feature. The `RecomputeScheduler` at vllm_ascend/core/recompute_scheduler.py:26 also imports `ECConnectorMetadata`, showing integration with Ascend's recompute scheduling path.

legacy_profiles.name: eplb.communicator
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter selects the communication backend used to transfer expert weights between GPUs during Expert Parallel Load Balancing (EPLB) rebalancing operations. The choice of backend directly affects the speed of weight transfers, which in turn impacts the latency of EPLB rebalancing steps and overall inference throughput when EPLB is enabled. On Ascend NPU, the "torch_nccl" backend relies on HCCL (via torch.distributed), while "torch_gloo" uses CPU-side communication. The "pynccl" backend is required for stateless (elastic EP) mode and provides lower-level NCCL control. The default is computed at runtime based on other EPLB configuration settings: "if elastic EP is enabled, it defaults to \"pynccl\"; if async EPLB is" enabled, it defaults to "torch_gloo" to avoid NCCL multi-thread conflicts; otherwise it defaults to "torch_nccl". On Ascend, "torch_nccl" maps to HCCL operations, and the vllm-ascend project has introduced a "pyhccl" communicator for direct CANN HCCL library calls, though it is not yet integrated into the EPLB communicator selection logic.

legacy_profiles.name: eplb.num_redundant_experts
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the number of redundant (duplicate) experts created during Expert Parallelism Load Balancing (EPLB). On Ascend NPU, it directly determines the total physical expert count: "n_physical_experts = n_logical_experts + num_redundant_experts." The physical experts are distributed across EP ranks, so increasing this value increases the per-rank expert count (n_local_physical_experts = n_physical_experts // ep_size), which proportionally increases GPU memory consumption for expert weights and KV cache. During EPLB rebalancing, redundant experts allow the balancer to migrate load without dropping tokens — insufficient redundancy causes load imbalance and throughput degradation. The vllm-ascend documentation explicitly states this value "Must match tensor-parallel size (e.g., 16 for 16 GPUs) to ensure sufficient redundancy." Setting it too low causes resource underutilization; setting it too high wastes memory and may cause OOM. In vllm-ascend's eplb_utils.py:76, when dynamic_eplb is disabled, n_redundant is forced to 0 regardless of the configured value. In upstream vllm, elastic EP scaling dynamically recomputes this value based on physical-to-logical expert mapping.

legacy_profiles.name: eplb.policy
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter selects the expert parallel load balancing (EPLB) policy used to redistribute expert weights across NPUs/GPUs in MoE models. The policy directly controls how expert-to-device mappings are computed from workload statistics, which in turn determines inter-device communication volume and expert load balance. On Ascend NPU, the vllm-ascend plugin provides its own policy implementations (policy_factory.py) that override the upstream vLLM policies. Policy 3 (flashlb) triggers a warm-up phase and uses a multi-stage algorithm (multi_stage=True in EplbWorker). Poor load balance causes some NPUs to be overloaded while others idle, directly reducing throughput. The rebalance algorithm's quality (measured by imbalance ratio, tested to be ≤1.08 for swift and ≤1.1 for flashlb) determines how evenly expert computation is distributed, which is critical for large MoE models like DeepSeek-V2/V3 running on multi-NPU Ascend clusters.

legacy_profiles.name: eplb.step_interval
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls how frequently expert parallelism load balancing (EPLB) rearranges experts across devices. In vllm/distributed/eplb/eplb_state.py:432-436, the step_interval is used to set self.expert_rearrangement_step_interval, which determines the number of forward steps between expert rearrangement operations. The initial rearrangement step is set to step_interval - step_interval // 4 (i.e., 75% of the interval), meaning the first rearrangement occurs earlier than the regular cadence. A smaller step_interval triggers more frequent expert redistribution, which can improve load balance and throughput at the cost of rearrangement overhead (communication and computation). A larger interval reduces overhead but may allow load imbalance to persist longer, degrading throughput. On Ascend NPU, the HCCL all-to-all communication used during expert rearrangement is particularly sensitive to frequency — too-frequent rearrangement can saturate HCCL links and hurt latency. The parameter also interacts with eplb.window_size: if step_interval exceeds window_size, only the most recent window_size steps of metrics are used for rearrangement decisions, potentially making frequent rearrangements less informed.

legacy_profiles.name: eplb.use_async
legacy_profiles.impact_detail:
This parameter controls whether Expert Parallel Load Balancing (EPLB) weight exchange uses non-blocking (asynchronous) communication. When enabled, EPLB weight synchronization between ranks runs in a background thread, overlapping with computation to reduce the performance penalty of load rebalancing. The mechanism works as follows:
1. In vllm/config/parallel.py:899, when use_async is true and elastic_ep is not enabled,
   the EPLB communicator backend is set to "torch_gloo" (instead of "torch_nccl") to avoid
   NCCL multi-thread conflicts that could cause hangs during async weight exchange.

2. In vllm/distributed/eplb/eplb_state.py:351, the async flag is stored in the EPLB state
   and used to determine whether weight synchronization runs synchronously or asynchronously.

3. In vllm/distributed/eplb/eplb_utils.py:73-103, when async EPLB is combined with the
   DeepEP low-latency all-to-all backend and an NCCL-based communicator, the code overrides
   NCCL_MAX_CTAS to prevent deadlocks caused by interleaved NCCL and DeepEP kernel launches.

On Ascend NPU, the impact depends on whether the HCCL communication library exhibits similar multi-thread conflicts as NCCL. The torch_gloo fallback may have different performance characteristics on Ascend compared to GPU. Async EPLB can improve throughput by hiding communication latency behind computation, but may increase memory usage due to additional buffers for non-blocking operations.

legacy_profiles.name: eplb.window_size
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: This parameter controls the size of the sliding window buffer used to record expert loads for Expert-Parallel Load Balancing (EPLB). In eplb_state.py:420-429, the value is read from `parallel_config.eplb_config.window_size` and used to allocate a tensor of shape `(window_size, num_moe_layers, num_physical_experts)` of dtype int32. A larger window_size increases GPU memory consumption linearly (each entry is 4 bytes × num_moe_layers × num_physical_experts) but provides more historical data for the load-balancing algorithm to make rearrangement decisions. The parameter does not directly affect computation time or communication — it only affects the memory footprint of the load recording buffer and the statistical quality of the load estimates used by the EPLB policy. On Ascend NPU, the behavior is identical to upstream vLLM since vllm-ascend does not override or modify this parameter.

The performance impact is classified as "low" because while the parameter itself does nothing on Ascend, the KV transfer subsystem it belongs to could theoretically affect performance if Ascend were to implement its own KV transfer backend in the future.

legacy_profiles.name: kv_transfer.engine_id
legacy_profiles.impact_detail: The engine_id uniquely identifies a vLLM engine instance for KV cache transfer (disaggregated prefill-decode or data-parallel KV sharing). On Ascend NPU, vllm-ascend patches the engine_id at startup by appending a UUID suffix (vllm_ascend/platform.py:389) to prevent collisions between co-located instances. In data-parallel setups, vLLM upstream further appends "_dp{rank}" (vllm/v1/engine/core.py:1094, vllm/v1/engine/utils.py:318). The engine_id is used by KV connectors (Mooncake, Nixl, Moriio) to register with bootstrap servers and route KV transfer requests. A non-unique engine_id causes registration collisions, preventing KV transfers and breaking disaggregated serving or DP KV sharing — resulting in failed requests or degraded throughput. The parameter itself is not directly user-tunable for performance gains, but incorrect configuration (duplicate IDs across nodes/instances) causes functional failures that manifest as performance degradation.
